Our findings indicate that parallel processing can substantially enhance matrix multiplication efficiency, outperforming sequential processing by a factor of over 650 on a single node with one processor. Furthermore, our research paves the way for exploring parallel algorithms in undergraduate computer science courses.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks that individual agents cannot complete on their own. We investigate the concept of coordination, focusing on a scenario where agents have restricted capabilities, including computation and communication limitations, within a pre-determined network structure. By applying a cyber-physical framework, we develop a method for analyzing the co-ordination time, representing the time it takes for the agents to complete a task together. Specifically, for a regular network with N agents, we derive the coordination time as a function of N, specifically as CPS (d_{max}/2 sqrt(2)), where d_{max} represents the maximum distance between agents within the network. This approach allows us to compare the efficiency of different network structures, as a regular network outperforms both a fully connected network and a star network in terms of coordination time for a large number of agents.

As precision strategies advance for future colliders like HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We examine the potential role of IR-enhanced amplitude-based resummation in achieving this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity.

This study examines the security concerns of vertical federated learning (VFL), a fed-
erated learning technique that combines data from multiple sources. VFL enables the
training of complex models that require sensitive information by multiple parties,
without the need for central data aggregation. However, this study highlights the
vulnerabilities of privacy in VFL, particularly in relation to the disclosure of training
details. It also highlights the risks of malicious activity, such as model inversion and
reversing the process, as well as the stealing of machine learning. Furthermore, the
study includes methods for achieving privacy in a practical way.

Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. A common workaround utilizes Random Fourier Features, but this approach has a significant drawback - it becomes impractical when data size increases, due to the extensive need for storage and computation associated with the large amount of feature mappings. A more efficient alternative presents itself in the form of a kernel estimation technique that leverages the unique characteristics of certain kernel functions, namely their ability to be represented as automatic relevance determination (ARD) models. By employing an efficient data-dependent method to update the ARD parameters during the training process, this approach enables the creation of approximate kernel functions that facilitate efficient dimensionality reduction while retaining the accuracy of the original method. Experimental results show that this technique achieves comparable performance to the method's precise counterpart while achieving a 4-5 order of magnitude increase in speed.

We investigate how groups that operate on sets in a recurring manner, specifically those defined by repeated applications, give rise to their natural expression within the wreath products over the base set. To this end, we introduce an innovative method called the Cartesian breakdown, which uncovers fundamental insights into this relationship. By exploring this relationship in various contexts, we gain a deeper understanding of how the structure of the group operating on the set influences the resulting group within the wreath products. Furthermore, this insight enables us to identify unique characteristics of groups that are invariant under changes to the operating set.

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by determining the conditions under which these conformally flat hypersurfaces can be scaled to have a constant Mobius curvature. Next, we establish that a compact subset of these hypersurfaces can be scaled to have a non-negative Mobius curvature. Additionally, we identify specific cases (including those related to Clifford tori and their great grandparents) where the scaled hypersurfaces can have a positive Mobius curvature. We also find that compact, non-toric subsets of these hypersurfaces can be scaled to have a non-constant Mobius curvature.

We evaluated the transferability of a specific type of deep learning network, U-Net, in cardiac muscle segmentations, specifically in cases of rare congenital heart diseases, using data from cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, by comparing its performance with a more established method known as the left ventricular mass rule. This comparison involved assessing the accuracy and reliability of the deep learning network, as well as its practical applicability for surgical planning. Further, we investigated the underlying reasons for its effectiveness, or lack thereof, in such transfers, and addressed potential issues with, bias, overfitting, and data quality. Our results showed the deep learning network's high level of precision, but some level of inaccuracy, and also the possibility of improving its performance with more training data. Moreover, we highlighted the need for more studies on this type of medical image analysis, particularly in low-data settings.

This research focuses on a specific type of microstructure within functionally graded materials, specifically aiming at modeling the strength decline of these materials. A novel model has been developed to represent this decrease in strength, where the model is based on the concept of decreasing grain orientation probability as you move from the center to the periphery. It has been proven that this model leads to a specific type of inhomogeneous material model that can be applied to any type of crystal structure. The model has the advantage of being computationally efficient because it uses the harmonic mean to calculate the strength, unlike other models that use methods like maximum/minimum. The model has been tested against numerical simulations and real-world experiments, showing that it can accurately predict the decline in strength. Additionally, the model has been applied to a specific type of material called bi-crystals, resulting in a 45-degree angle of weakness, which is in line with observations of materials like copper.

A new approach to efficient wireless communication is proposed in a multi-service system that utilizes SWIPT technology, allowing services to be powered and data-transmitted via wireless signals. The system consists of multiple Base Stations that serve various applications, with an centralized optimizer making decisions on a centralized platform. The optimizer determines the power distribution, rate allocation, and encoding schemes for a given dataset, with objectives that maximize overall network capacity and ensure that individual services meet their own performance requirements. To tackle this complex problem, the optimizer utilizes a multi-agent system, with each Base Station operating as an autonomous agent that makes local decisions based on its own data and collaborates with the centralized optimizer to adjust the system configuration and optimize performance. The system is evaluated under real-world conditions using a simulated dataset, with results showing that it is resilient to changes and can achieve optimal performance.

Object detection in an image is often considered complete after identifying all relevant bounding boxes. However, accurately classifying these boxes into the correct category is also crucial. This classification aspect is currently incorporated into the loss function used for training, with a focus solely on the final classification output of the largest box. This limiting approach overlooks the potential benefits of using information from smaller boxes. Our research suggests that these smaller boxes can contribute to the classification task and enhance overall model performance. To achieve this, we propose a new multi-box classification framework that enables the incorporation of a wide range of boxes into the classification process. This framework is versatile and can be seamlessly integrated into existing object detection models. Our experiments demonstrate that using this framework results in a significant improvement in model accuracy, with an average gain of 2.51% across the COCO benchmark categories.

Complex, multi-factorial datasets are increasingly being analyzed with Bayesian conditional models, due to their ability to handle large datasets and complex prior distributions without difficulty. While these models are effective, they lack a key statistical concept: extremal point analysis. As a result, researchers are unable to evaluate the extremal characteristics of the likelihood function, including the number of modes, and assess the behavior of posterior distributions in relation to the likelihood function's extremes. This study rectifies this shortcoming by incorporating an extreme value theory framework, enabling the analysis of Bayesian conditional models in conjunction with their limiting distributions of posterior quantities. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in identifying the number of modes, as well as providing confidence intervals for Bayesian estimates, even in the absence of computationally intensive methods. Furthermore, this study showcases its applicability to Bayesian autoregressive integrated moving average models and Bayesian neural networks.

We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding where identical word forms convey different meanings based on context. Although humans naturally infer word meanings from their context, machines struggle with this task. In order to tackle this issue, we can draw upon the vast amount of annotated data available, which incorporates a machine's interpretation of word context in relation to its meaning. Nonetheless, such datasets are scarce, primarily due to the intricate nature of WSD. As such, we'll leverage a more accessible approach, utilizing a BERT-based model called GlossBERT to assign word meanings based on context. We'll train and test this model on datasets containing annotated word senses within their surrounding context. Although previous approaches employed a fixed context length, we've adopted a novel method of determining the optimal context length for each word sense by considering various factors such as the number of words and characters within each sense, as well as its frequency of use. Nonetheless, we've discovered that utilizing a single, unified context length yields the most optimal results. Nonetheless, our experiments have shown that using a pre-trained model like BERT, combined with a suitable context length, significantly outperforms other approaches.

Reasoning about and completing procedures that involve multiple forms of communication (e.g., text, images, videos) is a key aspect of complex human expertise. To tackle this challenge, our research focuses on unlocking the natural language capacity to easily understand and execute detailed instructions delivered through various media. We've developed three key contributions to address this issue. Firstly, we've established a new representation that incorporates information about both the sequential nature of language and the structural elements found in various media. This representation allows for the completion of a diverse range of sequential tasks that involve multiple forms of communication. Secondly, we've created a strong neural network that can learn the sequential structure of complex human expertise from autodidactic guidebooks featuring multiple forms of communication. By using this expertise to sequence guidebooks, we've achieved impressive results on tasks such as movie dialogue prediction, medical procedure summarization, and cooking recipe generation. Our research demonstrates that learning about the sequential structure of complex human expertise is possible, and this knowledge can be applied in a wide range of applications involving the natural language ability to complete procedures that involve multiple forms of communication.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is analyzed in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors examine the effect of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, the time it takes and the number of nodes that become disconnected are calculated for a Cayley tree network. Moreover, the distribution of the number of nodes that become disconnected is derived and analyzed. Monte Carlo simulations are used to verify the accuracy of the theoretical calculations.

Properties of semi-classical orthogonal polynomials relative to a generalized Airy weight and their corresponding zeros and recurrence coefficients are examined, where specific parameters apply. The study extends to a symmetrized form of this weight known as the generalized sextic Freud weight, resulting in a parallel investigation of the associated polynomials' properties.

The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hampered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is crucial for detecting gravitational waves produced by binary neutron star mergers. We are proposing a new detector design, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which utilizes a novel approach to optical recycling. This design leverages the'sloshing' effect in Michelson interferometers to enhance signal-to-noise ratios at high frequencies, thereby improving detection capabilities in the 100-400 Hz frequency range. Our studies indicate that a 300-meter long detector employing this design could enhance the sensitivity by one factor of ten and boost the detection rate of binary neutron star mergers by 30% a year.

Recent research has shown that a protocol called XL-MIMO RAP offers significant improvements in real-time video transmission rates through large MIMO systems, achieving up to 9.5Gbps in an environment with 10 simultaneous connections. This protocol works by allowing each MIMO device to transmit a random access signal without prior coordination, taking advantage of the high number of possible signal dimensions in MIMO systems to significantly reduce errors and data loss. However, the XL-MIMO RAP protocol assumes that the MIMO devices' antennas form non-overlapping visibility regions, which creates a coordination problem as the devices move and their visibility regions change. This paper explores the mathematical conditions under which the devices' visibility regions will remain non-overlapping, developing an innovative approach to predicting the probabilities of the regions becoming overlapping as the devices move. The research also highlights the potential for applying its findings to other random access protocols.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have significantly enhanced our understanding of young star-forming regions' properties. However, the vertical scale of protoplanetary disks remains poorly understood, largely due to the absence of observational constraints in the 10-100 AU range. Our previous modeling demonstrated that the formation of substructures in protoplanetary disks, specifically in the inner regions, is compatible with a disk model exhibiting vertical shear instability. This model predicts the presence of substructures on a vertical scale of approximately 10-100 AU. The objective of this study is to provide observable predictions for the dust continuum based on the vertical shear instability model. We have developed a numerical algorithm for solving the Boltzmann equation and calculating dust temperatures in a vertical slab of protoplanetary disks. The assumptions made in this study align with those in our previous paper, specifically that the disk undergoes vertical shear instability and has a level of turbulence that does not impede the growth of substructures. The dust grains in this model are stratified according to gas density, located in the midplane, and subject to external radiation from their parent star. The temperature calculations obtained from our algorithm have been used to create mock observations for a range of frequencies corresponding to 230 GHz, 350 GHz, and 650 GHz. The features predicted by this study for the frequency spectrum are substructures in the 10-100 AU range, with characteristics that vary based on frequency, whereas the locations of substructures at

The term 'Big Apple Strength' is used to describe the latest observed spin magnitude in $^{48}Si$, specifically referring to its large separation energy for one-proton emission. This phenomenon raises interesting questions about the interplay between single-particle and collective motion in atomic nuclei. In a discussion that spans from medium-mass to open-shell grand unified field theories, researchers explore the underlying drivers of 'Big Apple Strength'. They examine potential explanations, including high angular momentum requirements, collective Scheel forces, and pairing-antipairing correlations. Furthermore, scientists consider the broader implications of 'Big Apple Strength' for understanding the properties of finite nuclei, neutron stars, and black holes.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, our investigation into SrMnO$_3$ highlights the significance of choosing correlated orbitals and constructing the lattice model. Using a Wannier-like approach, we demonstrate that considering only the correlated orbitals and constructing the lattice model using the Fourier transform results in a more coherent representation. This leads to a more coherent representation when comparing it to the traditional approach, thereby allowing for a more detailed analysis of the local and non-local interactions within the material.

This research focuses on creating resilient, uniform quantum gates for multiple qubits using trapped ions via the M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen process. To achieve this, a novel, balanced multi-mode circuit quantum electrodynamics setup is proposed, allowing for the efficient and stable application of quantum gates despite motion-induced fluctuations. A key aspect of this method is its ability to effectively use the multiplexing capabilities of motional modes in trapped ions to a significant advantage. Using this setup, our simulations demonstrate the potential to execute uniform quantum gates on up to five qubits simultaneously, reducing the necessary time by a factor of five compared to traditional methods while maintaining high fidelity levels (>0.999) for various gate times. Furthermore, this setup also offers the benefit of enabling controlled-phase M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates with high fidelity (>0.9995) for realistic scenarios involving motion-induced fluctuations.

Using advanced computational models, we investigated the underlying structures of certain paraelectric materials at the microscopic level. By leveraging machine learning to analyze large datasets, our approach revealed the unique atomic arrangements within these materials. Specifically, we identified the fundamental building blocks and their variations that make up the barium titanate (BaTiO$_3$) and potassium niobate (KNbO$_3$) families of perovskites. Our findings showed that these materials exhibit complex internal structures, comprising multiple variants of the fundamental building blocks, particularly when studied using high-resolution techniques that analyze small units of structure. These discoveries have significant implications for modeling the unique properties of these materials and might lead to new applications, potentially by combining materials with different structure sizes.

Lately, researchers have been looking for strongly correlated metals with Dirac fermions, which are rare in 4d spacetime. A 4d transition metal dichalcogenide layer, specifically its $h$-band, exhibits Dirac character, and strong electronic correlations are induced by local moment interactions in its band structure. Our analysis indicates that this system may enter a strongly correlated state with a self-doped Dirac spectrum, mediated by local moment-driven electron interactions and spin-orbit coupling. This prediction is based on a mean-field theoretical model which includes a self-dressed mean-field Hamiltonian to account for both local moment interactions and electron correlations. This approach is analogous to the $f$-sum rule, and it enables a coarse-grained description of the system's behavior using a single parameter, $U$, which represents the local moment interactions in the band. Our analysis of this model suggests that it exhibits a self-doped state with reduced electron correlation and a mini-Dirac spectrum, and we anticipate that this self-doped state may be achieved experimentally through isoelectronic substitution, which could potentially allow for the exploration of strongly correlated metals with Dirac fermions in 4d spacetime.

We present a new mathematical framework that can handle situations with two distinct sets of observations, where these observations are subject to varying success criteria. Our framework can be applied to any scenario involving independent and identically distributed data, and it enables the development of general methods for estimating nonuniform rates and proportions in bimodal data. Specifically, we demonstrate how our approach can be utilized to create estimators for a range of bimodal rates and proportions, including the p-value for uniformity, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, and the estimation of bimodal probabilities. Furthermore, we explore the properties of these estimators and provide empirical evidence to support our method's effectiveness.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production processes cannot adequately explain. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit.

In a Galilean frame, we examine the spectral shift phenomenon in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, focusing on an aircraft carrying the interferometer while moving at a constant velocity $v$. To calculate the spectral shift, we apply both classical and quantum theoretical approaches. The classical model considers the aircraft's velocity impact on light flow and calculates the spectral shift. The quantum theoretical approach, utilizing the Dirac operator with a non-invariant metric, yields a more complex calculation resulting in multiple spectral shift terms. One term is proportional to $v^2$, considered 'anomalous'. This anomalous term contributes to the system's energy and doesn't depend on light's frequency. It may cause a spectral shift in energy levels of a quantum system inside the moving aircraft. The anomalous term is connected to the Sagnac interference effect, which arises when light travels in opposite directions through the moving aircraft. The term 'anomalous' is used here because it implies the existence of a non-trivial spectral shift that isn't dependent on light's frequency. The name 'anomalous' originates from Eotvos' experiments searching for this spectral shift in relation to the Sagnac effect. The quantum theoretical approach shows that the 'anomalous' term can be seen as a consequence of the Sagnac interference effect. The name 'anomalous' will be replaced by a more descriptive one, such as 'Sagnac', in the full version of this paper.

This work extends the findings of Cox and Hunter, specifically regarding parabolic adjoints, Weierstrass sections, and nilfibres in type $A$. We begin by identifying a Weierstrass section for flag varieties associated with algebraic groups of type $A$. This enables us to determine the structure of the nilfibre, or more precisely, a part of it, in a precise and detailed manner. Moreover, we establish a connection between the parabolic adjoint action and Weierstrass semisimple elements. The approach employed builds upon the work of Preston, whereas the results obtained generalize those of his research.

Neural language models have significantly contributed to various natural language processing tasks, consistently demonstrating an advantage over traditional $n$-gram models. This study delves into the underlying causes of this performance difference and proposes a novel understanding of language as a hierarchical structure of $n$-gram blocks. Building upon this foundation, we introduce a neural text generation framework called NgramBLM, which learns neural representations while refining linguistic structures through a self-supervised learning approach. By incorporating a token-level language model, NgramBLM enables the generation of multiple sentence candidates for each token, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance in various evaluation metrics for machine translation and language modeling. Moreover, NgramBLM excels in adaptability, proving particularly effective at low-resource and domain adaptation settings.

We've developed new principles for categorifying the $\mathbb{Q}$-polynomial functors introduced by Kostant in 1963, utilizing the language of $\mathbb{N}$-semiring varieties and Grassmannians. Our approach enables us to prove a significant categorification of the $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano version of Kostant's theorem, a key milestone in the study of representation theory. This advancement builds upon the foundation established by the first author in his previous work, where he explored $\mathbb{N}$-Fano categories and established connections to Laurent polynomial rings and their extensions over fields of one variable.

Reconstructing and aligning 3D faces in complex real-world images has proven challenging due to frequent occlusions, varying lighting conditions, and different image formats. These issues make reliable 2D-3D face alignment and reconstruction a difficult task. To address this problem, we've developed a pioneering approach that tackles these challenges by designing two novel modules tailored for self-alignment and self-healing of faces in images. Our approach uses a self-alignment module to account for slightly misplaced landmarks during 2D-3D alignment and a self-healing module to repair broken tetrahedrons during 3D reconstruction. By integrating these modules, we've created the SADRNet framework capable of executing both tasks simultaneously. To ensure accurate evaluation, we've assembled a vast dataset consisting of 50,000 images and obtained multiple models to perform around 1.3 million 2D-3D face alignment and reconstruction procedures with a median error of 5.3 mm, surpassing current methods and demonstrating the SADRNet's effectiveness.

We investigate the consequences of combining symmetries that are both spatial and translational in nature. The efficient field theories that arise from this combination can lead to fractonic phenomena when some of these translational symmetries are broken spontaneously. Our study explores how the low-energy properties of these systems give rise to dimensions of fractonic mobility that are less than full, specifically half-dimensional for both one- and two-dimensional cases. These low-dimensional mobility fractions arise from the combination of spatial symmetries and the efficient descriptions that result from integrating out unnecessary degrees of freedom. We also demonstrate that certain dimensions of mobility can be manipulated by applying external forces, leading to the emergence of new modes of motion. These new modes can be thought of as 'hall effect' movements that occur even in the absence of a external force when there is only one spatial dimension present. Lastly, we examine how sound modes that couple with the fractons can lead to the formation of stable fixed points when both the fractons and sound modes display power-law behavior.

In the early stages of the universe, specific types of $\alpha$-attractor inflation models experience a sudden disruption in their symmetry, resulting in an oscillatory phase. This oscillatory phase can result in the creation of primordial black holes if it leads to the local formation of over-densities during the universe's evolution. We examined the potential for universe over-densities to form during the oscillatory phase of $\alpha$-attractor inflation, focusing particularly on models where the phase of symmetry breaking is marked by a disturbance that cannot be dissipated. We discovered that in these models, the formation of both generic and tunneled black holes becomes more likely, with the probability of tunneled formation being significantly higher if specific initial conditions are met. The formation of both types of black holes is facilitated by the universe entering a phase of contraction during the oscillatory phase, a process that is more likely if the inflationary network is composed of multiple-unit cells. This raises the possibility that a substantial quantity of universe over-densities could be generated during the oscillatory phase of $\alpha$-attractor inflation, with implications for the distribution of masses in black holes formed in this manner.

A marked ordered tree (MOT) is an ordered tree where specific nodes are designated as targets. The set of target nodes is denoted as V. A path in a MOT is the sequence of nodes connected by edges. The deepest vertex in a path is the node furthest from the root. If a path has an odd number of nodes, the deepest vertex is the rightmost node. If a path has an even number of nodes, the deepest vertex is the leftmost node. Not all MOTs contain a deepest vertex, as it depends on the number of nodes in the longest path. However, the term "deepest vertex" is well-defined for all MOTs.

The counting process for US election ballots, whether conducted manually or via a machine tabulator, relies on a complex system of holes punched through paper, which is then subjected to optical character recognition or a human count of marks on a ballot tally. This study proposes a third option, Informed OCR, which combines the advantages of both methods. By utilizing a machine learning algorithm to identify the layout and content of a ballot, this approach enables the accurate conversion of marks on a ballot tally into votes. This method excels in low-light environments, at a larger scale, and when counting historical elections, outperforming the accuracy of human counters.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring parameter efficiency. However, it has been observed that certain time series models, despite being over-parameterized, tend to perform better with fewer estimates. This research explores a range of linear time series models that achieve low error rates even with highly precise estimation methods, including over-parametrized autoregressive models. We demonstrate that these models inherently possess a level of robustness, reducing the significance of model selection in relation to the true data generating process. Furthermore, we show that cross-validation-based methods can efficiently take advantage of the models' robust nature by facilitating achievable interpolation errors. This allows us to leverage the benefits of over-parameterization, thereby facilitating optimal combinations of frequency and asymptotic bias in model performance.

This paper presents a new deep learning architecture, which integrates a complete attention mechanism with bidirectional elements to upgrade the performance of single-channel speech enhancement. The proposed architecture utilizes a complex neural network to model the supplemental attention between frequency bins, leveraging a non-linear representation to supplement the traditional bidirectional recurrent neural network with a limited attention range. Furthermore, this model incorporates multiple bidirectional long short-term memory elements to expand the attention range, allowing for the integration of medium- and long-term contextual information. Experimental results show that this architecture yields superior performance to conventional deep learning techniques, outperforming them in terms of signal-to-noise ratio in 0.13-0.35 dB, 0.14-0.37 dB and 0.11-0.34 dB for short, medium and long test sets respectively, and also excels in subjective quality and naturalness.

A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and inducing a significant discrepancy in pressure readings, potentially compromising the containment of hazardous pathogens. Our research suggests implementing a more sophisticated method of pressure regulation that is less susceptible to frequency-based attacks.

A key factor in microgrid functionality and effectiveness is the ability to store energy. We refer to the ability to do so as a'storage' function, present in both physical and nonphysical forms. We examine how risk-averse market participants self-allocate their storage capacity under uncertainty, both individually and within a decentralized framework. In the decentralized setting, we model other microgrid participants as competing risk-averse market participants. We use stochastic representations of uncertainty and the storage function to formulate a stochastic optimization problem. We leverage duality and variable splitting to solve this problem, obtaining an efficient and feasible solution. We go on to investigate the implications of our results for microgrid management, particularly in regards to self-allocation of storage under uncertainty. We use numerical examples to illustrate our approach and the benefits it confers.

X-ray pulses can initiate intense electron motion within matter, and studying this process is critical for advanced metrology and manipulating electron waves. Unfortunately, conventional methods used to investigate electron dynamics are limited by the short duration of the associated processes. In contrast, He-like ions offer a unique opportunity to examine electron dynamics due to the longer timeframe of Auger decay, which is influenced by electron motion. A novel approach is presented that utilizes ultra-short, pulsed light to excite He-like ions, and the resulting temporal evolution of the Auger spectrum is used to demonstrate the potential for time-domain studies of complex electron systems. Parametrizing a quantum mechanical model with experimental data allows for the direct extraction of essential parameters that describe the electron dynamics. A notable feature of this method is its high temporal resolution, with results indicating that the electron wave function's temporal behavior is consistent with a small effective mass and a particular sign of the anisotropy parameter. Furthermore, this approach may be applied to study electron dynamics in other systems using x-ray free-electron lasers.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that appear in experiments with medium rotation rates are similar to mid-latitude storms observed on Earth.

Deep neural networks for object recognition have consistently shown improvements, with a marked increase in the depth due to the adoption of transformation-based layers. Despite this, significant room for growth remains, as the existing architectures struggle to fully exploit the information contained in ImageNet. In order to overcome this limitation, we have designed a novel type of layer called the Hierarchical Transformation Block (HTB), which is capable of complex transformations while being highly efficient. By integrating multiple instances of the HTB across several layers, we have created a deep learning architecture known as the Hierarchical Learning Architecture (HLA), which has achieved the best-ever ImageNet classification accuracy of 79.3%. This architecture has not only set a new benchmark but has also demonstrated that deep learning is highly effective at image recognition, surpassing the previous best result set by a significant 3.5% over the existing best deep learning performance.

In this work, we are analyzing a linear time-invariant system whose stability is evaluated using the algebraic and spectral properties of its matrix representation. A key concept in this evaluation is the algebraic multiplicity, and we are specifically exploring its connections to the system's dynamics. We have derived a novel formula for the algebraic multiplicity in terms of the system's transfer function and Routh characteristics, as well as its geometric interpretations on the complex plane. This formula provides a clear link between the system's poles, its reduced normal form, and its Lyapunov eigenvalues. We have also established a correlation between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric properties of the system's critical contours, specifically those defined by the Routh criterion. These connections shed new light on the algebraic multiplicity and can be very useful in addressing stability issues for linear and nonlinear systems.

We suggest creating pairs of correlated bosons using large numbers of long-lived dipole-like atoms that interact with an optical cavity. A rapid growth of entanglement between these atoms, driven by a combination of light-matter interactions and spontaneous emission, can result in the production of paired states. We demonstrate that this process is capable of generating squeezed light, even when there are significant losses. We also examine the potential for this phenomenon to contribute to optical homodyne measurements beyond the Heisenberg limit.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a comprehensive computational model of two-electron behavior in silicon has been created by applying a multi-valley effective mass approach. This model accurately predicts the electronic configuration, overlap, and exchange interaction properties for pairs of qubits placed in different locations within a silicon crystal. It also simulates the effects of nearby surface nanoscale etchings that can influence valley mixing. To speed up development, a useful rule of thumb for exchange energy optimization has been established. To validate the model, its predictions for certain scenarios were compared with experimental measurements, showing a good level of correlation. Although this model can be applied to any silicon donor pair, it is particularly designed to model pairs of phosphine-donated silicon qubits, for which exchange energy optimization has been successfully demonstrated.

Our investigation focused on the conductance of a mercury telluride quantum well near its critical thickness, where the band structure changes from an insulating to a semiconducting nature due to the reversal of the Galvanomagnetic and magnetotransport signs. Despite expectations for the conductance to drop off as the quantum well approaches its critical thickness because of the gapless nature, our measurements reveal that the conductance remains steady, driven by the unique properties of the Dirac fermions that arise in this specific thickness range. A theoretical model showing that the conductance is controlled by the singular distribution of Dirac points has been developed and successfully used to create a universal graph that can predict the conductance in any given magnetic field by identifying the position of the quantum well in a plot of magnetoresistance versus magnetic field.

Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals, we develop a mathematical model for calculating the outage probability of the ACN protocol and provide analytical expressions for the results. By applying special limit cases, we can better understand the protocol's efficiency. Numerical simulations confirm our theoretical findings, highlighting the ACN protocol's superior performance over traditional VC methods.

In our research, we're addressing an important problem in 5G and future wireless communications. Due to the system's ability to switch frequency into different time slots dynamically, there's a conflict between maximizing spectral efficiency and minimizing service delay. This conflict becomes more pronounced when there are many devices competing for time slots. We've developed a method called the model scheduling approach, which allows a base station to make decisions about scheduling in real-time. By modeling the system's performance as a function of scheduling decisions, we've created a game-theoretic framework that can learn the system's parameters and maximize its performance. We've also considered several factors that affect the system's performance, including the delay factor, power control, and a form of fading known as Nakagami fading. We've evaluated our method's performance through simulations, and the results show a significant improvement over other approaches. We've achieved a 50% reduction in delay and a 20% increase in spectral efficiency with our method. Notably, our approach is more efficient, taking only one-thousandth of the time it takes for other methods.

Despite numerous theories, there has not been a clear understanding of the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors, particularly in their mixed-state Hall resistivity. This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving through the lattice within close proximity to the vortex cores. This proposed mechanism is to be tested against two theories commonly accepted in the field: the time-reversal symmetry-breaking theory and the chiral-vortex-antivortex pair theory. Our analysis aims to provide quantitative evidence in support of the vacancy motion theory and contrasts it with the two established theories. Furthermore, this study involves an evaluation of Zhao et al.'s experimental findings from the perspective of vacancy motion and identifies key parameters that align with the vacancy pair motion model, thereby offering a quantitative framework that can be utilized in analyzing future experiments designed to test this concept.

Using an advanced statistical approach called the maximum likelihood estimation, researchers re-examined existing magnetic data from two types of materials with magnetic properties that change as temperature varies, known as spin glasses and ferromagnets, specifically focusing on how the magnetic moment's value affects probability distributions in these materials under different temperature conditions.  By analyzing likelihood ratios, researchers identified specific temperature points where the distribution's shape remains consistent despite changes in magnetic moment's value, also known as fixed points.  Additionally, as temperature decreased, researchers observed an expansion of probability distributions across all measured intervals, a phenomenon some scientists associated with the onset of magnetic order.  Furthermore, a distinct fixed point was found in ferromagnetic materials at a higher temperature than in spin glasses, indicating differences in the magnetic properties of these materials, with some scientists linking this to the presence or absence of competing interactions in these materials.  A more detailed analysis of probability distributions in these materials under different temperature conditions may provide further insights into their magnetic properties.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of matrices that generate a finite-depth subfactor is based on Galois extension properties, specifically the square's invariance under the central quotient action of its centralizer, which is equivalent to the square's index being a power of an odd prime, resulting in the subfactor being a powers of a specific prime-depth hyperfinite type $II_1$ factor, accessible via the Shimura tree.

Recent research has introduced self-bounding Hamiltonian Neural Networks, generating precise outputs within a confined range, identical to the input range. This property seems impractical at first, but it actually facilitates the creation of feasible solutions to optimize complex objectives, including those involving derivative calculations. To illustrate this, we transform the problem of computing derivatives into an equivalent Hamiltonian dynamics problem, taking advantage of the network's inherent ability to produce bounded outputs. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on synthetic data and real-world problems requiring the computation of gradients. Our approach provides a framework for enhancing training stability and efficiency, also making it possible to train models with calculated gradients using only Hamiltonian Neural Networks, bypassing the need for explicit gradient calculations.

As artificial intelligence becomes ubiquitous, understanding the underlying machine learning models is essential for building confidence in their decisions. Our proposed framework incorporates a two-pronged approach to address this issue. Firstly, it utilizes a collaborative method to provide explanations for model predictions. Secondly, it employs a collaborative method to refine the models through data augmentation based on the confidence levels of the users. The objective of this approach is to enhance the reliability of the machine learning models.

In x-ray based prohibited items detection, the challenge lies in balancing detection speed and accuracy. Despite the significance of this issue in ensuring airport security, few studies have addressed it. To enhance the quality of evaluations, a new dataset called High-Quality (HQ) has been created and released in conjunction with this study, comprising 10 categories of prohibited items with over 18,000 high-quality annotations, spanning 5 datasets. The HQ dataset serves as a superior alternative to existing datasets and facilitates more rigorous evaluations of prohibited items detection methods. A novel module called the Lateral Inhibition Module has been designed and integrated into an object detection framework with limited latency, yielding state-of-the-art performance on the HQ dataset and outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy.

We create a novel quantum invariant, denoted as $V_Q$, for links in a thickened torus. $V_Q$ is constructed using the Kauffman bracket network evaluations on a modified version of a link in $S^3$, specifically based on the Volume Hypothesis. Notably, tests reveal that $V_Q$ can distinguish between some links that have the same crossing number but are not visually similar, thereby demonstrating that cross-eyed versions of the trefoil and figure-eight knots possess distinct invariants $V_Q$.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine contextual and lexical knowledge for more effective WSD.  This study focuses on enhancing the Context-gloss Pair dataset, which is commonly employed for testing WSD systems.  Initially, a more comprehensive data set was created by incorporating additional context-gloss pairs derived from Wikipedia, along with three well-known BERT-based WSD systems.  Subsequent experiments undertaken to evaluate these systems, utilizing both the original and enlarged Context-gloss Pair dataset, revealed that they performed better on the expanded data set.  A crucial finding emerged, showing that the existing methods tend to select the most frequently associated sense with a particular word, indicating a potential shortcoming of these approaches.  Notably, one method demonstrated a reliance on the training data set's biases, thereby highlighting the significance of thoroughly examining the underlying characteristics of data sets employed for evaluating WSD systems.

The reciprocal Gamma function is analyzed in this paper, where a distinguishing factor $x$ in the complex plane is introduced, leading to the derivation of a regularized Hankel-type integral representation. Additionally, a novel connection with the classical Hankel-type integral representation of the Gamma function is established via a limiting process.

This study investigates the production of top quarks in proton-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV and 8.16 TeV, considering three distinct ranges of top quark masses spanning from 400 GeV to 900 GeV. Our analysis focuses on the top quark and the accompanying bottom quark being centrally produced and rapidly moving in the same direction, commonly referred to as the "same-sign" dilepton signature. Our analysis reveals that the production of top quark pairs can be differentiated from proton-proton collisions' production in events featuring same-sign dileptons, specifically at an 8 TeV top quark mass. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the interaction between the top quark and the large skewness of the proton's field can result in the production of the top quark in a manner that depends on the component of the quark's spin, thereby providing a unique perspective on the role of spin in quark production.

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL research, specifically handling null values and selecting the best join order. To tackle this challenge, we're proposing a novel approach that builds upon existing work by Han et al. and involves three key components: a cross-domain text-to-SQL system and two auxiliary tasks. This approach is unique in its handling of null values and join orders, leveraging pre-trained language models and logical operators through two separate networks. This approach has achieved impressive results on the SuperGLUE dataset and has shown significant improvement over baseline models in null value handling and join order selection. Furthermore, this approach has led to a 20% reduction in null values and a 10% faster execution time on average. This study is significant because it's the first cross-domain text-to-SQL research and has made available a dataset split into training and testing sets. This approach has also made available pre-trained models for both Spirte and Hanftask tasks in the code repository.

This paper delves into the challenges and limitations of applying differential privacy to protected entities within a broader network. It examines various statistical approaches established for private data analysis, highlighting their difficulties in handling complex network data. Furthermore, the paper discusses the limitations of differential privacy in preventing targeted attacks and sheds light on the limited availability of dataset owners' cooperation in private data sharing. Additionally, it outlines promising research directions for the next phase.

The vast image database and impressive scientific outcomes of the Euclid mission will make it an influential leader in the field of cosmology for years to come. To fully realize the potential of these images, significant computational resources are needed to process them efficiently. This prospect assesses the computational challenges Euclid will face and explores the opportunities for the ADAM processing unit to meet these demands. It also examines various strategies for ensuring the longevity of Euclid data and making its valuable scientific outcomes accessible to the broader community.

In this research, we propose an automatic method to generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. A similar descriptive tool could enhance the experience of listening to music playlists. Building on the foundation of visual captioning, music captioning would provide a new way for users to engage with playlists. In this paper, we introduce a novel application of music captioning: narrating music playlists. It describes a system that generates written descriptions of playlists, producing both verbal and visual explanations. We examine various input features and model configurations, ultimately presenting a proposed system design. Furthermore, we outline potential research extensions in this field.

Researchers have recently developed a random hydrodynamical approach to describe the dynamics of Bose gases interacting via short-range forces, using a microhydrodynamics method that connects microscopic randomness to macroscopic fluid dynamics. This approach reveals how interactions influence the hydrodynamics, causing a random quantum fluid to deviate from classical behavior and display correlation effects reminiscent of superfluidity. Utilizing this framework for a quasi-condensate phase, investigators have identified the long-term behavior of hydrodynamic correlations and found that they conform to a linearized kinetic equation, offering a practical means to investigate correlated quantum fluids using hydrodynamics.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for enhancing temporal action detection. DCAN aggregates dual contexts through two separate pathways: a self-context pathway and a semantic context pathway. Our self-context pathway is designed to capture the long-term temporal context by aggregating adjacent context boundaries, while our semantic context pathway is designed to produce proposals with adjacent semantics. We further integrate these two contexts to prevent proposal duplication and improve distinctness. Notably, our approach is distinctive in its use of dual context aggregation, unprecedented in prior boundary matching methods. Our method has achieved exceptional results, outperforming state-of-the-art methods like BTI in the ActivityNet v1.3 and ActivityNet v1.4 datasets with significant improvements of 5.6% and 4.4% in average recall at 0.25, respectively.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation centered on ELM filaments themselves. It is proposed that the formation of a PTM results from the superposition of multiple ELM filaments with distinct magnetic field velocities, which in turn leads to the observed features characteristic of a PTM, such as a peaked edge current density and a large magnetic shear within the mode. This theory is supported by computational simulations and observations from high-speed cameras, which show that the current density within a PTM closely resembles that of an ELM filament just as it is about to interact with the bottom of the lower bumper. It is also predicted that the duration of a PTM is equal to the time it takes for a filament to complete one rotation, which is consistent with experimental data.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for multiple mobile robots moving dynamically in a confined space by employing dynamic vortex potential fields. Our approach leverages vortex potential fields, initially proposed as a method to guide robots around each other in circular trajectories, and adapts them to handle robots moving along linear paths. To account for changing robot positions and velocities, their potential fields are continuously updated, and a priority system is established to direct robots with higher priority indices to navigate around those with lower indices. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through simulation testing.

Consider a long sequence of letters generated randomly from an alphabet, where nearby letters are drawn together to form n-dimensional bundles representing words of length n. A fundamental frequency associated with these word frequencies governs their distribution. A large deviation principle is established for the relative entropy of the frequency distribution within a given phrase, relative to a reference distribution that reflects the average frequency of such phrases. The specific frequency patterns that lead to extreme deviations from this average are characterized by a rate function that measures the likelihood of such events, and it takes the form of a Legendre transform. The model includes dependencies between letters within a word, allowing the frequency distribution to depend on the underlying metric structure of the alphabet. A key component of the frequency distribution is a measure that captures the correlation between letters within the sequence. A second large deviation principle is established for the correlation matrix itself, and it is characterized by a scaled Boltzmann-Gibbs measure that reflects the most improbable correlation matrices given the frequency matrix. The models explored in this study are relevant to the analysis of genomic sequences, including prokaryotic and eukaryotic genomes, as well as literature, where the frequency of words and their underlying algebraic structure may convey important information.

Recent advancements in the field of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) are providing innovative solutions to various signal processing challenges. One such potential application is a radar system that utilizes an IRS to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper presents a comprehensive mathematical model of a radar system with an integrated IRS and derives the optimal reflective coefficients of the surface via the minimization of the mean squared error (MMSE) method. We also demonstrate the potential of the proposed radar system to significantly improve target parameter estimation in scenarios involving limited access times. Furthermore, the paper incorporates simulation results to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in scenarios with single and multi-target configurations.

Universal fuzzers such as American Fuzzing Toolkit (FTA) significantly expand the reach of fuzzing, reducing the expertise required and significantly increasing its potential for discovering vulnerabilities. Nonetheless, these tools raise concerns about the effectiveness of fuzzers being testbed dependent. While they have successfully uncovered vulnerabilities in various contexts, it is unclear how they perform in other situations. To address this uncertainty, we are changing the perspective from a positive to a comparative approach, focusing on how to contrast and quantify the discovery rates of different fuzzers. We have developed a methodical evaluation process for assessing the effectiveness of fuzzers, demonstrating its utility through a case study where we employ it to examine the variability in discovery rates of FTA on various programs, as well as the impact of program characteristics on the effectiveness of its core algorithms. Our research also reveals surprising insights, including the inefficiency of one critical algorithm, leading us to consider ways to enhance the performance of modern fuzzers.

Pretrained models have been highly effective in various continued learning scenarios. Yet, it has been discovered that a straightforward approach, which fine-tunes a basic model for sequential learning tasks without leveraging the pretrained models, shows surprisingly competitive results in many cases. We examined the underlying reasons for this simplicity working so well and discovered a couple of key factors. Firstly, the natural order of tasks typically presents increasingly diverse samples, which aligns with the inherent challenges of sequential continual learning. Secondly, the inherent task structure is often reflected in distinct subspace components, allowing for efficient incremental learning. We utilized these insights to analyze the success of the simple baseline in various tests, and our analysis sheds light on the critical elements that make the baseline effective. We also explored the possibility of applying related strategies to other continual learning challenges.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for a map between metric spaces, specifically tailored for surfaces. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of minimal surfaces within a given relative homotopy class in a metric surface. The existence of such minimal surfaces is guaranteed if the map lies in a simply connected relative homotopy class. If the map is also locally injective, we can demonstrate the uniqueness of the minimal surface. This theoretical framework has the potential to be applied to substantial problems in geometric minimal surface theory.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data are $u(0,x)=\phi(x)$ and $u(0,x)=\psi(x)$, are examined with specific properties of the function $f$ as we explore their large-time behavior. If $x$ is distant from zero, the solution $u$ is defined in terms of the equilibrium $u_\infty$ over a critical period. If the function $f$ is differentiable and the initial data $\phi$ and $\psi$ are convergent, the solution $u$ will eventually become $u_\infty$ as time approaches infinity. Additionally, if the derivative of the function $f$ is negative for values between $u_\infty$ and $\phi$ or $\psi$, the solution $u$ will also converge to $u_\infty$ over a certain period. If the function $f$ is sublinear, solutions corresponding to initial data with distinct limits will converge to the unstable equilibrium $u_\infty$. If the function $f$ is polynomial, solutions corresponding to initial data with distinct limits will converge to the unstable equilibrium $u_\infty$ for values less than $\lambda_1$, and will converge to a periodic solution for values greater than $\lambda

Recent studies on 64Ni, a proton-rich nucleus with a low-spin structure, have shed new light on its shape coexistence properties. Based on a Monte Carlo shell model, our research examines the influence of the monopole interaction on proton and neutron pairs in 64Ni. We find that the monopole interaction between like particles plays a crucial role in determining 64Ni's zero-spin ground state, driving the coexistence of shape-invariant configurations found at higher spins. Our analysis suggests that the combination of pair interactions and the 1g9/2 proton hole's configuration is vital in understanding 64Ni's low-spin coexistence phenomenon.

Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a class of games known as Lipschitz games, which involve unique equilibria that are isolated from mixed strategies played by a significant number of players. Their work demonstrated that these games have the power to create unique, isolated equilibria even without any assumptions about the underlying space. In addition, they established that a particular subclass of Lipschitz games can result in equilibria that resist a substantial number of questions before being accurately identified. However, the problem of determining whether all Lipschitz games can create question-resisting equilibria, as well as the specific question of whether a particular subclass of these games can result in equilibria that can only be correctly determined after being queried a large number of times, both remain unanswered. Furthermore, we have previously shown that a particular subclass of Lipschitz games can result in equilibria that can only be correctly determined after being queried a substantial number of times. This work builds on that by providing new lower bounds, which demonstrate that both a particular subclass of Lipschitz games and the underlying space can result in equilibria that can only be correctly determined after being queried a large number of times.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are often simply the result of low variance estimates due to the luck of draw in the CV process, rather than truly indicative of the model's ultimate performance. We contend that the traditional approach of averaging the results of multiple CV iterations to inform parameter tuning is flawed, as it tends to overestimate the benefit of reduced variance. As an alternative, we propose a simple modification to the CV procedure that involves using a J-K fold cross-validation design. By introducing an extra layer of randomness into the CV process, this modified design reduces performance estimate variance while minimizing the risk of overfitting. We demonstrate the efficacy of this modified design in effectively guiding the selection of optimal model parameters, particularly in scenarios where the optimal path is not well defined.

In recent years, a student-instructor architecture has been widely adopted in knowledge-based learning models, particularly in generative models that utilize two separate components: a student that generates data and an instructor that guides the student through corrections and feedback. This architectural setup has yielded significant gains in various applications by facilitating efficient two-player minimax learning. Despite its effectiveness, the rational behind using this architecture in conjunction with generative models is not well understood, often being recognized as an empirical phenomenon. This survey paper delves into the rationale behind the success of student-instructor architectures in knowledge-based learning, exploring connections to the concepts of risk minimization, as well as the epistemic and ontological risks present in deep learning models. Additionally, the paper discusses various design considerations and future research directions for the student-instructor architecture in knowledge-based learning.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. This framework, titled Brief Function Representation (BFR), employs a limited set of operations to define a function based on its individual components. We have discovered that utilizing BFR, we can perform the maximum probability estimation (MPE) calculation, a critical task, as well as other optimizations, significantly faster than other methods. Additionally, BFR is capable of handling constrained MPE calculations, which is an important application in various domains. Our evaluation demonstrates that BFR outperforms existing methods for both exact and approximate MPE calculations, particularly in scenarios involving structured activities and object detection.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern shifts from 0.107 cm$^{-1}$ to 0.213 cm$^{-1}$. This phenomenon arises from the transfer of momentum from the photon to the atom during absorption, a phenomenon that becomes more pronounced as the intensity of the light increases. Our findings are consistent with theoretical predictions and provide a foundation for using cold atoms as a tool for studying the scattering of light.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of liquid materials exhibit sudden changes in behavior characterized by a sharp increase in viscosity. This phenomenon, known as shear thickening, can result in the development of rigid structures within the liquid at high shear rates. However, the underlying causes of shear thickening remain poorly understood and are dependent on multiple factors such as particle interactions, friction levels, and the presence of polymers. In this study, we investigate the relationship between shear rate, structure, and mobility within a dense suspension of polystyrene particles in polystyrene, a material that undergoes significant structural transformations during shear thickening transitions. Our analysis of processed X-ray tomography data allows us to measure the changes in structure and track the mobility of particles during shear thickening, ultimately revealing a universal scaling that defines the behavior of materials at the point of shear thickening. This scaling indicates that the mobility of particles is constrained by the size of structures formed during shear thickening, and we find that this relationship holds true for both the onset and point of shear thickening, shedding new light on the microscale mechanisms driving this phenomenon.

The paper introduces a new algebra variant called the Racah algebra, which is a central extension of the tensor product of two simple algebras by means of the second integer derivative of the Euler partition function. It establishes that the centralizer of the action of the symmetric group on the tensor product of two representations of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ corresponds to a specific subalgebra of the Racah algebra, and proves that this centralizer generates a sequence of finite-dimensional representations with a Hilbert-Poincaré property. Additionally, the paper defines another variant called the Weyl-Racah algebra, which is a central extension of the symmetric square of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ by means of the first integer derivative of the Euler partition function, and demonstrates that it is closely related to the Racah algebra through a finite-dimensional quotient.

Our study shows that in a layer of hexagonal magnets with a small interlayer distance, there's a possibility of achieving magnetic long-range order and universal superfluid or supersolid behavior tied to a gapped excitation called the triplon. To model this, we used a Monte Carlo simulation for a classical Heisenberg model with a layer symmetry constraint. The results indicate that in the presence of strong easy-axis anisotropy, magnetic order and superfluid/supersolid behavior both emerge. Specifically, the triplon modes become gapped when there's antiferromagnetic order, allowing for superfluid/supersolid phases at low temperatures. Moreover, we found that magnetic order and universal superfluid/supersolid behavior can coexist, resulting in a twisted supersolid phase with a triplon gap and van Hove singularities in its density of states. This occurs when there's a particular relationship between the triplon wavevector and hexagonal magnet's lattice spacing. This provides a theoretical foundation for exploring twisted supersolid phases in magnetically gapped systems using deep laser absorption spectroscopy.

This study examines 3D WIMP-nucleus scattering events as they relate to the recoil angle distribution, specifically how the incident velocity affects this distribution. Our simulation reveals that for most nuclei, the velocity's impact is minor, yet it results in a notable energy dependence. Consequently, attempting to infer the WIMP mass based on this distribution alone may be misleading, at least for heavier nuclei. Furthermore, this analysis applies to both slow and high-energy events. Additionally, we found that the recoil angle distribution is closely linked to the energy spectrum, particularly for smaller nuclei where this connection holds true over a wide energy range. Nonetheless, this correlation may break down below a certain energy threshold due to detection limitations.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as one-quarter of the participants may lose crucial information due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, the potential risks it poses, and the necessity of training all professionals who work on the Web on how to use search engines effectively.

We are exploring the concept of a cutting-edge particle collider that could revolutionize our understanding of high-energy physics and possibly uncover the fundamental theory behind it. This report outlines the potential of a muon collider, which could provide unprecedented insights into Higgs boson research and offer a groundbreaking perspective on supersymmetry, in addition to presenting a compelling case for its development.

A new technique is proposed to create high-quality, respiratory motion-free 4D T2-weighted MRI images from multiple scans taken during different phases of breathing. The proposed method develops a mathematical model to predict breathing patterns and uses machine learning to correct for variations in breathing, eliminating the need for patients to follow a specific breathing routine. The technique includes algorithms to remove cardiac-induced motion and adjacent organ encroachments from images, and it also offers flexible spatial resolution adjustment. The proposed technique was compared to a conventional 4D MRI technique in terms of diagnostic accuracy and image quality, using data from 30 healthy volunteers and 30 patients with abdominal pathologies. The results showed no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy, but the proposed technique produced higher-quality images with less artifacts.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing secure control systems for autonomous vehicles with limited sensing capabilities. Specifically, it outlines a methodology for creating control barrier functions using state constraints and feedforward control, ensuring the safety of the vehicle in complex dynamic scenarios. Additionally, it presents an efficient algorithm for implementing this design method efficiently.

This paper introduces the concept of CF-approximation spaces, a new regional representation approach that encompasses both CF-representations and A-approximation spaces. Our research shows that there is a direct correlation between CF-representations and A-approximation spaces, proving this relationship holds true for any given region and refining the definition of CF-representations in the process.
