Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals, our findings indicate that even relatively simple approximations can produce accurate power spectral density (PSD) fits, specifically using quadratic expressions for the likelihood function in terms of eccentric binary parameters. Conversely, more precise models, such as those based on post-Newtonian relations for the power spectral density, may not significantly improve the quality of fits, especially when constrained to highly eccentric orbits, and may instead require excessively lengthy computations in their current form.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a velocity process emerges which conforms to a specific type and is capable of moving to the right over a finite distance before reversing direction. Additionally, we determine the exact probability distribution of this velocity process at any given point in time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the case of ASEP with exclusion and the presence of extra particles moving at twice the speed of regular particles, a coexistence phenomenon arises where the velocity process can consistently move to the right over an infinite distance, and we establish the probability distribution of this velocity process as well.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, a range of methods has been proposed to identify and clarify acronyms within written content. However, existing techniques fall short in providing a comprehensive solution that users can trust, mainly due to the absence of a unified benchmark for evaluating acronym identification and disambiguation techniques. To address this gap, we present MadDog, a web-based platform that enables users to test their acronym identification and disambiguation algorithms through a user interface and utilizes a unified evaluation framework to assess the performance of submitted models.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversions in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. Furthermore, we demonstrated that applying a light-based association field at the optimal point can achieve $\sim 90\%$ efficiency in converting spin atoms to molecule pairs. When the dark-state condition is not met perfectly, we developed a random photon-atom system model to model recoupling and obtained stable atom-molecule pairs from initial spin atoms via a process influenced by collisions that transfer spin and light-based association. Lastly, we explored the influence of light-based association and described the transition from a collapse to a stable coexistence of atoms and molecules through adjustments to a key parameter.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new method for creating a hierarchical structure on DNA, enabling efficient data updates. To address this challenge, we've developed a new sequence-manipulation technique and an updated encoding scheme. Our simulations demonstrate improved performance with larger data sets, achieving faster query and update times compared to existing solutions.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to increase awareness about nodal lines by explaining their unique topological characteristics and recent realizations in photonic and other systems. It highlights the unique properties of nodal lines, discusses various types found in theory, and explores recent developments in photonic, phononic, metamaterials, and electrical circuit realizations, also touching on potential applications utilizing these systems. Furthermore, it outlines the basic design requirements for creating nodal lines in artificial materials and suggests potential for further exploration in nodal lines.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate. 3D MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning. However, interpreting MRI images can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists. Developments in deep learning, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), have significantly improved automatic tumor segmentation and classification accuracy. A multi-task learning approach is the most effective way to combine the tasks of segmentation and classification. Notably, radiologists primarily focus on identifying the tumor region and its type, making it crucial to develop a system that accurately performs these tasks. In response to this need, we propose a novel, multi-task directed network called MAG-Net, which incorporates an attention mechanism to direct the network's focus on both tasks. We utilized the multi-region, multi-task learning approach with MRI data from the Figaya challenge, and the Segmentation Evaluation Metric (SEM) was employed to assess the network's performance. The findings show that the proposed MAG-Net model yields a SEM score of 0.8346, outperforming the current state-of-the-art model, demonstrating its superiority. Furthermore, the classification component of the model achieved a remarkable 92.85% accuracy.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance optimization-based methods, particularly those that rely on differentiable objectives. However, incorporating real light sources into the rendering process poses a significant shadow computation challenge, as casting and detection become ill-posed problems due to ambiguous source-surface interactions. Existing differentiable methods for shadow computation are limited by their sensitivity to noise, poor performance in complex scenes, and inability to account for multiple light sources. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel differentiable shadow computation framework that differentiates not only the rendering process but also the shadow itself. This framework leverages a composite model that integrates implicit representations of both surfaces and light sources. To tackle the issue of source-surface misalignment during shadow casting, we develop an analysis-inspired method that utilizes both the Sobolev embedding theorem and the Lipschitz constant to achieve robust results. Our approach is capable of handling multiple light sources and complex scenes, and is efficient enough for integration into optimization-based inverse problems through differentiable pipelines.

Ancient TV systems, like the ones from the 1920s to the 1980s, employed interlacing scanning to transmit video, inserting alternate rows of scan lines in a frame. This resulted in distorted video playback, particularly noticeable in moving objects, and a common issue known as "comet tail." A frequently used remedy was the application of a motion compensation algorithm in a process called motion interlacing, often resulting in over-correction and the introduction of artificial patterns. In an effort to address these issues, a new method has been developed, Real-time Deep Motion Interlacing, utilizing convolutional neural networks to accurately detect and fill in missing scan lines in video frames, with the ability to process 720p and 1080p video in real-time.

We investigated the influence of different approaches to density constraints on the characteristics of neutron distributions in various relativistic and non-relativistic mean field models, excluding the constraint on density. A comparative analysis was conducted between models that use the standard density constraint and those that use the constraint based on the incompressibility modulus, specifically within the relativistic mean field model and its non-relativistic density-dependent mean field model counterparts. A specific example was examined using the relativistic mean field model with an isospin asymmetric density constraint and a simple density-dependent non-relativistic mean field model. A notable finding from this analysis was the relatively small impact of different density constraints on the characteristics of neutron distributions, especially when compared to the significant influence of theoretical model type. It was observed that the characteristics of neutron distributions are quite similar across different models, often exceeding the differences by an order of magnitude. Consequently, the average square radius of the neutron distribution is largely model-dependent, in contrast to other characteristics that are only moderately model-dependent.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for avoiding deadly drowning accidents and facilitating safe river exploration. Although the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions, such as the full-Galery-Kinematic-Linkage method, are time-consuming and require precise riverbed geometry information. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that rapidly solves the shallow water equations using deep learning, enabling the prediction of river flow velocities at high speeds (-25 times faster) than traditional methods, including the full-Galery-Kinematic-Linkage method. In oursupplementary website, we have made available our code, which can be tried out against the data we used for training and validation.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to
encompass a broader range of illumination. This process can be both time-consuming
and difficult to achieve optimal results using a smartphone's automatic exposure
control. A novel approach is presented that makes use of a smartphone's raw data
captured over a set exponential exposure levels. Our method involves taking four
images with standard and double exposure values. These images are then fused using
a technique that prioritizes the most illuminated pixels in each one. The resulting
images are merged into an HDR image through a weighted average of the captured
images. Advantages of this method include the ability to obtain high-quality HDR
images using a smartphone, reducing the necessary capture time, eliminating the
need to adjust camera settings, and producing consistent results. The method has been
successfully tested and the results validated by a photography expert.

Causal experts and machine learning specialists tackle two disparate challenges: unraveling the intricacies of causal networks and developing reliable models of probability. Two notable frameworks, Bayesian networks and Gaussian graphical models, have demonstrated exceptional utility in both fields. However, the community has thus far failed to integrate the methods used to construct these frameworks, leaving a significant gap in our understanding. We aim to bridge this gap by drawing from a wealth of research in both causal networks and machine learning. We begin by illustrating the inherent structural assumptions made by various models of probability, such as Gaussian graphs and Bayesian networks, and then examine their inherent assumptions about causal relationships. We establish a clear distinction between models that incorporate both structural and causal information and those that only utilize structural information. We also explore the benefits of incorporating prior knowledge about causal relationships when estimating these models and discussing the difficulties that arise in doing so. Ultimately, we outline a unified approach to constructing models that incorporates both causal and structural information, referred to as causal learners. This framework allows for the representation of causal relationships that are represented by directed acyclic graphs and facilitates the generation of posterior distributions of models that are consistent with these relationships. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to the analysis of Gaussian data with hidden factors, showing that it yields results that are on par with state-of-the-art methods while also allowing for the estimation of causal relationships. Our approach also offers the benefit of being able to handle large datasets and is therefore an ground-breaking advancement in the field.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of in-situ rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to study the temperature distribution within a sand bed heated from above, showing that the formation of thermal arches develops and shifts over time as indicated by water's freezing point at different locations.  Our temperature mapping technique was validated using thermocouples and demonstrates the development of two-to-three distinct thermal zones within the bed during both laminar and turbulent flow conditions.  The findings also indicate that the formation of thermal arches enhances heat transfer efficiency in both flow regimes, particularly in turbulent flow where the increase in heat transfer is more substantial.  Our study highlights the potential of in-situ MRI temperature mapping in investigating the dynamics of thermal processes and mixing patterns within porous media.

This note presents a weakened version of the b-principle for maps with singular targets, tailored to cover the congruence classes of maps that are relevant in the Madsen-Weiss theorem, specifically the conjectures related to the manifold extension and the surface extension parts of the MW theorem. We also discuss an application to prove the congruence class version of the Strominger conjecture, a key component of which is a weakened version of the 2-dimensional Mumford Conjecture.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

The study of unitary invariant ensembles of complex matrices with the property that the absolute value of the entry at position (i,j) is the same as the entry at position (j,i), has seen significant progress in recent years. Specifically, statistics of standard matrix entries have been understood when conditioned on having the same value for the conjugate. This paper explores an extension called "autonomous matrices" where entries at positions (i,j) and (j,i) are independent, not equal in absolute value. It is shown that conducting the same conditioning yields independent families of probabilities, parametrized by the angle theta, which include beta and gamma distributions. Additionally, results are derived for singular value statistics and the largest absolute entry.

Persuasive video generation, an emerging field in computer graphics and multimedia research, has seen significant growth in interest over the years due to its potential to influence public opinion through visual content. This area has caught the attention of academics working at the intersection of artificial intelligence and human behavior, who are motivated to explore the possibilities of creatively shaping public perception. This survey paper provides an in-depth examination of the theory behind persuasive technology and the emergence of persuasive multimedia, as well as various AI-driven approaches to creating persuasive videos through text, image, and video. Additionally, it discusses the challenges associated with evaluating the effectiveness of persuasive videos and offers potential avenues for research in this field.

Users often rely on system-generated security indicators to assess risks, which can be misleading due to various attacks. Our proposed framework, designed for operating system environments, aims to provide users with accurate security notifications. It offers a notification system for users to correct their perception of security and provides educational content to enhance users' understanding of computer systems. Our approach was tested with college students, and the results showed that users' confidence in security was reduced, but their knowledge of operating system vulnerabilities increased following the workshop.

Recently, acoustic metagratings have been proposed, offering a versatile way to manipulate wave properties through periodic structures. We've successfully created a microacoustic metagrating at ultrahigh frequencies (approximately 250 MHz) using three-dimensional photolithography, achieving remarkable unit cell density down to 39% due to customized geometries. A comprehensive theoretical framework based on the scattering matrix method accurately models this phenomenon, predicting a metagrating designed to concentrate sound waves. Our experimental results correspond with simulations, visibly demonstrating the concentration of an incident wave through our microacoustic metagrating at ultrahigh frequencies.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the possibility that spatial variations change over time, leading to a new model where the product rule is applied. This results in the average squared displacement growing linearly with time, and a specific non-Gaussian probability distribution. We examine this model in relation to anharmonic potentials and a specific protocol, and find that it applies and produces the predicted probability distribution.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between modes in optical resonators and waveguides. The framework is highly versatile, allowing it to be applied to a broad range of geometries and configurations. Building upon the qubit model, this new approach uses a circuit quantum electrodynamic-like formalism to derive equations that accurately capture the behavior of linear and nonlinear systems. The resulting theory encompasses multiple applications, including parametric amplification, non-linear metamaterials, and optical parametric oscillators. Furthermore, this theory provides a unified framework that enables a comparison of different optical resonator and waveguide systems, potentially leading to breakthroughs in technology.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic stability, Lyapunov functions, and control systems. We specifically explore a category of control systems characterized by continuous and unbounded control inputs, leading to the regulation of a differential equation with potentially unbounded inputs. The relationship between this class of control systems and Lyapunov functions is examined, with the condition of controllability being both necessary and sufficient for the existence of a local asymptotic controllable Lyapunov function. The paper also investigates a broader control system that includes those with smooth, continuous, and unbounded controls, resulting in the asymptotic stabilization of a differential equation. The association between this class of control systems and the concept of a global asymptotic controllable Lyapunov function is examined, with the condition of controllability being both necessary and sufficient for its existence. Moreover, the paper demonstrates the existence of a specific global asymptotic controllable Lyapunov function when the control input is smooth and bounded.

A novel deep learning approach was introduced that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed, high-resolution images from lower-resolution ones, tested on turbulent flow visualization at different Reynolds numbers. A comparative study was conducted to examine three types of discriminators and two types of generators in a generative adversarial network, leading to the development of an enhanced adversarial network with a composite discriminator and affine generator. This customized network successfully created high-resolution images from measurements taken at various spacings and Reynolds numbers, demonstrated through visualization, velocity profiles, and energy spectra. Furthermore, the model's accuracy was validated by comparing its outputs to actual measurements at spacings that the model was not trained for, showing promise for its potential use in super-resolution flow visualization and reconstruction of flows from limited measurements.

The article addresses the variational principle's application to determine the energy levels of a hydrogen-like atom, employing the method of undetermined multipliers to derive both the quantized energy levels and the electron density distribution, resulting in the well-known probability function $\left(r/R\right)^2e^{-2r/R}$.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the models' inability to account for the concept of open-world uncertainty, which encompasses all possible classifications in addition to the initial training data. This research proposes an innovative framework that addresses this challenge by incorporating an auxiliary energy-based function into maximum likelihood estimation. This energy-based component enables models to model open-world uncertainty and adapt to new data seamlessly, producing a more nuanced uncertainty distribution that outperforms existing methods in benchmark datasets.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to adapt to shifts in the environment, whether these changes arise from new task requirements, natural evolution, or deliberate modifications. This difficulty highlights the importance of assessing a reinforcement learning model's ability to evolve and adapt over time, across various contexts, as does the L2E framework, which introduces rigorous, comprehensive evaluations for both individual tasks and overarching methodologies. L2E features an adaptable design, encompassing diverse testing settings, rigorous metrics, and user-friendly tools to facilitate the comparison of different methods and a collaborative pursuit to address fundamental challenges in lifelong reinforcement learning.

Understanding business processes relies on process analysis, detection, and exploration methods. While existing techniques for declarative process discovery and analysis use complete data sets, our approach leverages real-time event data to monitor and explore processes. We define a declarative process model that enables identification of process instances and their completion times based on event attributes. Our approach and a related technique are evaluated using artificial and real event data, showing our method's effectiveness and efficiency. Our approach and the evaluation data are included in the supplementary materials. Additionally, we discuss potential applications and challenges for our approach.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden transition from localization to non-localization. Our theory demonstrates that in photonic quasicrystals, light localization can shift to a non-localized state as the symmetry of the system changes from even to odd. Additionally, we found that in some cases, localizing the system's initial state leads to a non-trivial, non-localized state. This phenomenon causes a reentrant shift of the localization transition as the system's symmetry changes from odd to even. We found that in photonic quasicrystals, light localization can shift to a non-localized state as the symmetry of the system changes from even to odd. This reentrant shift of the localization transition as the system's symmetry changes from odd to even is unique to one-dimensional quasiperiodic systems and has no equivalent in periodic systems.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering a vast field of view, Liger gathers extensive data, amounting to over 100 gigabytes per night. To handle this significant output efficiently, we've devised the data processing system to be based on the data management framework provided by the Observatory. To ensure a seamless operation with the observatory's systems, we've established software interfaces supported by modern interfaces such as the Joint Architecture for Scalable Software. These interfaces provide connectivity to the data processing system components and facilitate communication with the observatory's existing infrastructure.

Optical systems are increasingly dependent on the multi-dimensional analysis of quantum states of light. While Garrison-Killough's method offers a practical approach for solving the quantum problem, it comes with a significant limitation in its application to quantum communication - a severe light power constraint. Unfortunately, the high power requirement of classical source devices makes this method unsuitable for most communication scenarios. In our study, we propose the use of a bi-photon spatial mode demultiplexing system that significantly reduces the required light power while maintaining high resolution. The system's effectiveness was verified in a $64\times64$ channel demonstration. The BPSK source device used in our experiment operated at a relatively low light power of 10 mW, enabling the demultiplexing system to achieve a high spatial resolution of 6.5 λ2dr in 6SMD. This breakthrough may soon enable the practical application of high-dimensional quantum communication.

This study expands the moduli spaces of polarized varieties through algebraic and analytic means, focusing on a broad category that includes domains of abelian varieties, type X domains, and F-rational Landau-Ginzburg surfaces. It also examines rational connections on vector bundles over these expanded moduli spaces, particularly when the base space is a product of projective lines. It is shown that when the product has an infinitely long first component, this expansion does not change the cohomology group. When all components are finite, the cohomology group is still unchanged if a certain condition is met. It is also demonstrated that when the product has an infinitely long first component, the expanded moduli spaces can be expressed as a non-trivial product of the original moduli spaces and a certain analytic space. When all components are finite, the expanded moduli spaces can be expressed as a non-trivial product of the original moduli spaces and a certain algebraic scheme if a certain condition is met. It is proven that when the product has an infinitely long first component, the expanded moduli spaces are non-trivial if a certain condition is met. It is also proven that when all components are finite, the expanded moduli spaces are non-trivial if a certain condition is met.
