In complex ecosystems, population dynamics are often characterized by rapid fluctuations and slower trends, and identifying early warning signs in these systems can be crucial. We investigate the long-term behavior of a model representing a two-species ecosystem with intraspecific competition, predicting that certain abrupt population changes can be indicated by a shift in the system's transient activity. Our analysis reveals that major population shifts occur when the system's stable population equilibrium changes, and we develop a statistical method to detect this event by analyzing the transient dynamics. We apply this approach to a simulated data set and find that it effectively identifies population changes before the actual event occurs. Furthermore, we analyze the underlying mechanics of the ecosystem model using a reduced dimensionality approach, and our results demonstrate that our detection method is robust and accurate in a variety of scenarios.

We investigated the cause of the turning point in the star formation main sequence at high-mass galaxies, specifically the role of nuclear starbursts in dust-enriched cores. Using near-infrared data from Hubble Legacy Advanced Camera for Surveys Wide-Field Imagers, we localised nuclear regions in  5044 galaxies across 1.5 billion years of redshift and identified the critical moment when the main sequence relationship with mass begins to decline. Our findings show that nuclear regions start to contribute significantly to mass-to-star formation rate ratio at $M_* \sim 10^{10.5} M_\odot$ and turn over at $M_* \sim 10^{10.8} M_\odot$ mass thresholds, which correspond to the points where nuclear starbursts in dust-enriched cores emerge. We discovered a nuclear main sequence defined by $M_{\rm nuclear}/\rm SFR_{\rm nuclear} \propto M_{\rm nuclear}^{0.24}$ and found it to be more steeply sloped than the global main sequence. This increased mass ratio in nuclear regions suggests a critical mass where gas dynamics shift from orderly star formation in disks to merged masses in nuclear regions, leading to a transition in mass-to-star formation rate relationships.

This paper conducts a cross-language sentiment analysis to classify the emotions expressed in a given text, using a neural network that learns from data in two languages. We used a hybrid approach, combining both multilingual and single-language models, to develop a neural network capable of classifying the sentiment in two languages. We then employed a multi-task learning technique to extend this model to two new languages. Our results showed that the model's performance improved significantly when trained on three languages compared to training individual models for each language separately. Notably, our paper achieved the best score in the Sentiment Task at the 2019 Cross-Lingual Natural Language Processing Workshop's BERT-Base Multi-Lingual Task.

Cache coherence protocols employ self-invalidation and self-downgrade techniques to efficiently manage cache validity during repair operations. We examine the effectiveness of these protocols in scenarios where data can be stored across multiple memory modules, leveraging self-invalidation and self-downgrade to minimize downtime and performance losses. We evaluate the cache hit rates and repair times of three protocols - sequential, parallel, and distributed protocols - using self-invalidation and self-downgrade in scenarios with two to eight memory modules. Our analysis reveals that the sequential protocol achieves optimal results when data is evenly distributed across memory modules, while the parallel protocol excels in scenarios with unequal data distributions. We also propose a hybrid protocol and demonstrate its performance in relation to the sequential and parallel protocols.

In 1991, Freiman established a foundational result, stating that if sets A and B of size k satisfy certain additive properties, specifically Chabauty's four-term theorem, then sets consisting of k/4 elements from A and B respectively will also meet those criteria. Over time, various improvements have been made to this result, and we have further refined it to also cover situations involving near-progressions, a key area of study in additive combinatorics.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(f(t) + B^{H}(t) + c)_{t\in A}$ has a non-empty interior for the sup-norm on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. This is accompanied by a measure-theoretic result: if the Lebesgue measure of $A$ is positive, then so is the Lebesgue measure of the image $(f(t) + B^{H}(t) + c)_{t\in A}$ for almost all $\omega$ in $\Omega$.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on a quantum-dynamical description that incorporates symmetry properties. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Wick's type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculation of the energy and its associated uncertainty reveals that quantum fluctuations result in the breaking of symmetry, causing the ground state to become unstable and rotate in circular orbits.

X-ray images of patients with COVID-19 hold significant potential to prevent overwhelming of critical care units due to unnecessary admissions.  Although existing research primarily focuses on distinguishing COVID-19 from other lung conditions using X-ray images, our work aims to explore the possibility of identifying critical care unit candidates directly from these images.  By analyzing X-ray images of patients with severe COVID-19 who required immediate life-saving treatment, our system accurately predicted the need for urgent ICU admission in 93.75% of cases, serving as a foundation for developing an automated triage system using X-ray images.

The universal simplicial collection is a fundamental concept in the theory of simplicial objects, serving as a universal construction. It has far-reaching implications in categories of simplicial presheaves and simplicial functors. A significant breakthrough has been achieved in simplifying the universal simplicial collection when working with simplicial functors, for which categorifable objects yield a simplicial group, while those that do not yield a simplicial group requiring the use of the coproduct over categories of simplicial sets. Additionally, the universal simplicial collection of a simplicial presheaf on a category of simplicial sets results in a simplicial group if the presheaf is able to be categorized over all simplicial sets.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of erroneous positives in several ways. Firstly, it implements an innovative balanced sampling technique, sampling easier negative proposals in proportion to the difficult ones. This is achieved by utilizing a balanced categorical cross-entropy loss function. Secondly, we incorporated a spatial attention mechanism within our model to enhance performance on challenging proposals. Our method demonstrates superior results when compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques in the Visual Relationship Detection category, reducing the false positive rate by a significant 10% without compromising the false negative rate.

This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that's effective even in poorly lit video frames. Our action recognition model is delta-sampled, where we analyze video frames relative to the initial image, and employs a BERT-based RFB network for accurate classification. We trained the model with limited, low-light video data and tested it on three challenging video datasets, and our results show it surpasses the state-of-the-art in action recognition accuracy for dark video frames.

Current CPU designs, centered around instruction sets, diverge from the fundamental structure of programs which are comprised of interconnected operations aiming to produce specific outcomes. This discrepancy creates inefficiencies in how programs are executed, limiting potential performance gains. Our proposed Content Addressable Concurrent Processor architecture bypasses instruction decoding, allowing programs to be defined naturally as sets of functions working in tandem, and executes them directly through reverse evaluation. This led to a 2.5 times increase in performance and a 3 times decrease in code size when applied to benchmark programs, when compared to an optimized FPGA implementation using VHDL.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy.

We investigate a popular, semi-analytical model that explains the universal texture of the neutrino flavor matrix. This model, initially proposed by King and Segrè, suggests that neutrino oscillation parameters are directly linked to the elastic scattering of neutrinos on electron scattering. We reevaluate this model using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method for greater statistical precision. Our analysis confirms the semi-analytical results, and for two key variables, we find values consistent with the original predictions. However, we identify larger uncertainties in the remaining variables' values, primarily due to the limited experimental constraints. We also explore an alternative approach based on a direct relationship between neutrino flavor mixing and elastic scattering, reexamining this approach with the benefit of updated data sets.

We investigate a specific nonlinear elliptic equation involving a critical exponent, specifically in the presence of a non-homogeneous term representing a heat source. Our primary objectives are to prove the existence, local uniqueness and periodicity of solutions in a particular functional space. Notably, our existence proof employs a novel technique using the superposition principle, while our uniqueness proof relies on the local coercivity of the equation's operator. Additionally, we establish conditions under which the periodic boundary conditions are well-defined and demonstrate the implications of these conditions on the equation's solutions.

Current cutting-edge neural program generators excel in small-scale applications but often fall short in large-scale domains due to the complex dependencies involved. To overcome this limitation, our proposed approach, NeuralProgramGeneratorModuloAnalysis, leverages static analysis to break down the code generation process into more manageable tasks, thereby allowing the use of multiple specialized models to create the program. By doing so, we can generate programs with up to 5 times more functions compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, while also dramatically speeding up the code generation process. Our model, tested on the Microsoft MakeCode platform, demonstrates a remarkable 28% increase in accuracy, along with a 50% decrease in errors, when evaluated against a diverse set of 5000 test cases.

Recently discovered solar neutrino data from 2004 indicates a significant statistical anomaly, showing a notable difference in neutrino detection rates between two monitoring methods used by the Super-Kamiokande experiment. Analysis of this discrepancy, observed on November 7th, suggests a duration of approximately one hour, with the divergence increasing by 10% per hour. This anomaly cannot be explained by existing solar neutrino theories, particularly the MSW solution. One hypothesis proposes an alternative solution, involving the conversion of neutrinos within the solar core. However, this theory has limitations, as it only accounts for neutrino conversion during the core's central region. Another hypothesis emerges from the Snowball model of massive stars, which predicts the conversion of neutrinos in multiple solar core layers. Nonetheless, both of these hypotheses struggle to accurately replicate the observed data, leading researchers to consider the possibility of hadronic interactions within the solar core, as supported by recent observations of solar gamma rays.

The first order relativistic hydrodynamics is a closed system that linearizes to a wave equation, and this closure also holds in the presence of viscosity. By solving the equations of hydrodynamics for fluctuations around a stable equilibrium, we determine the dispersion relations and their corresponding wave patterns for both viscous and ideal fluids. We find that viscosity significantly alters the sound wave dispersion, transforming it from a quadratic to a linear relation in the fluid's rest frame, while temperature gradients influence the fluid's behavior in both cases.

As continuous-time approximate discrete-time time-series data enters the system, the existing anomaly detection techniques face challenges due to their static nature. To address this issue, we've developed an continuous-time anomaly detection framework that can handle streaming data. This framework can determine whether the data is following a specific pattern by calculating the quantum distance between two sets of features. It utilizes an exponential moving average to update parameters in real-time, effectively handling incoming data. This approach can identify anomalies in real-time, and we've evaluated it against seven well-known discrete-time anomaly detection techniques, resulting in superior performance.

A court-ordered disclosure of encrypted information poses an interesting problem. The holder of the information is compelled to reveal the contents, but maintaining the security of their access method is also the holder's responsibility. This paper explores possible solutions to this issue, focusing on a scenario where the holder's identity is unknown to the authorities requiring access. One potential approach involves leveraging homomorphic secret-sharing schemes, enabling the computation of encrypted information without revealing the underlying data. Another approach looks into using code-based solutions, such as code-based decryption methods and multi-party computation, to facilitate the revelation of information while upholding security standards. A code-based solution featuring code-based decryption protocols and MPC is presented, along with an examination of code-based schemes' efficacy in addressing this problem. Furthermore, this paper discusses code-based solutions' implications on trust relationships between individuals and authorities, highlighting the importance of clear guidelines and regulations to maintain those relationships.

This paper suggests a flexible simulation tool for measuring the efficiency of a measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD system) based on partial linear operator. The proposed model can simulate various quantum channels and device imperfections. It uses a unique approach to describe the positive operator-valued measure (POVM) used in measurement processes. The model can also handle non-linear channels and classical corruption of the system. The authors demonstrate the applicability of their model by using it to analyze a conventional QKD system and a system affected by linear and classical noise. The model can be used to study the trade-off between the gain and error rates of QKD systems.

We have designed a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) that can be applied to a broad category of discrete optimization problems involving non-linear objective functions and constraints, specifically those that can be efficiently computed and where certain key variables can be efficiently determined. This category encompasses numerous classic problems, such as multiway cut problems, minimum elimination ordering problems, and minimum-aggregation problems, especially those defined on graphs, trees, and their various substructures. Our PTAS leverages a novel combination of problem-specific aggregation techniques and bi-criteria approximations to achieve better scalability than previous PTAS algorithms for such optimization problems.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical approach for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The method is grounded in the Lagrange-Galerkin method and yields exact conservation of the equation's invariants. A direct consequence of this approach is the development of a conservative, high-order numerical scheme for the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, a key component of mean field games systems. The method's conservative property ensures that the solution's characteristic curve tracks the Hamilton-Feynman flow accurately. This strategy can be viewed as a conservative approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, and is efficient in modeling monotonicity properties of the potential function. The method has been tested against a set of benchmark problems, and is found to be particularly effective in scenarios where high order accuracy is required.

Advancements in deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved impressive performance in various complex tasks, often surpassing traditional techniques and becoming indispensable in everyday life. Nonetheless, the complexity of these circuits has reached the point where attempting to study their behavior is no longer feasible. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that numerous crucial decisions made by the circuits in critical situations, such as the release of suspicious financial transactions and suspected criminals' identities, are impossible for humans to understand. As a result, there is a growing need to develop methods to visually present and logically explain the decisions made by these networks. This survey seeks to offer a thorough exploration of both the visual representation and the explainability of DNNs. We will delve into various visualization techniques that make the neural network's learning process more transparent, as well as different approaches to provide the context for the network's decision-making process. We will also examine the benefits and drawbacks of these methods, in addition to outlining some promising directions for future research in this area.

The detection of spinning surface layers in several solar-type stars challenges our current understanding of their internal dynamics. This phenomenon is thought to result from the consumption of a planet, as seen in the destruction of planetary systems around white dwarfs, or an unexpected increase in angular momentum within the star's convective envelope. We investigate the possibility of enhanced angular momentum transport due to turbulent processes within the convective envelope, a scenario that could lead to the star spinning rapidly at its surface while slowing at deeper layers. This idea is supported by measurements showing that the convective turnover time in upper layers is faster than in deeper layers, which could contribute to the star's surface spin. If this process holds true, it could have implications for the survival of planets during the main sequence, potentially allowing for the destruction of smaller worlds where the star's convective envelope comes into play.

False news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although online platforms have implemented measures to combat false news, there is still a need for effective methods to detect it. To address this issue, a new approach called false news ground truth (FN-GT) is proposed, consisting of labeled training data that includes both true and false news articles, along with their corresponding emergence times. A novel false news detection framework called the meta neural process network (meta-NPN) is introduced, capable of learning to model the emergence of false news articles as functions of past data. Evaluating the proposed framework on the FN-GT dataset, it demonstrates superior performance to traditional machine learning methods and showcases its adaptability in handling real-world false news articles. Furthermore, the meta-NPN framework is shown to be more efficient, achieving a high accuracy rate of over 92% on the FN-GT dataset.

This research paper examines a transport equation featuring cyclic in its velocity field, the study is conducted in a domain with bounded capacity. We have demonstrated that if the initial data exhibits minimal discontinuity, specifically with one component being differentiable, then there is a finite period of time during which the solution remains continuously differentiable. We have also shown that if the velocity field's integral is zero, specifically demonstrating it in a two-dimensional space, then the singularities that develop are periodic.

This paper examines a discrete time status refreshing system with a Ber/G/1/1 queue to determine the age of information. We analyze the AoI by considering the time elapsed since the latest update was received and model it as a recursive process. To maintain the AoI at an optimal level, we develop a strategy based on the queue length and update interval, incorporating the arrival process's probability distribution. We prove that this approach minimizes the AoI's expected value and explore its efficacy in scenarios where the update interval is optimal for reducing the AoI. We also investigate the expected value of the AoI under optimal update intervals and derive an closed-form formula for its minimization. Furthermore, we apply the proposed strategy to a specific use case, the optimal AoI for an M/M/1 queue, and demonstrate its superiority over existing methods. Simulations are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a specific type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific types of algebras and by identifying additional constraints for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research greatly expands our current understanding of set-theoretic solutions and their quantum equivalents, revealing new general patterns in the field.

Recently, Golay complementary arrays (GCAs) have gained significant attention due to their utility in signal processing applications, particularly those utilizing polyphase orthogonal transformations. This paper contributes an exhaustive analysis of full-dimensional GCAs, specifically those composed of multiplephases, and offers a novel design approach for implementing them in rectangular forms. A key aspect of this work involves establishing a relationship between certain binary constructions and their corresponding multidimensional GCAs. We have created a set of phase-shift transformation matrices that can efficiently generate GCA forms in both rectangular and non-rectangular configurations. These designs encompass all possible phase arrangements and can be applied to both prime and composite dimension cases, providing a versatile framework for various signal processing applications.

Quantum tunneling is a phenomenon where particles exhibit non-intuitive behavior 
by passing through solid obstacles due to their wave-particle nature. This phenomenon 
can be utilized for coherent spin state generation and quantum computing applications. 
Although tunneling rates are typically measureable, researchers aim to explore the 
atomic-scale component of this phenomenon. Employing advanced scanning tunneling 
microscopy and atomic-scale electrical manipulation techniques, we studied the 
quantum tunneling of charge in silicon using silicon tips. Our findings reveal that 
tunneling enables the interference of valley states and spin swapping at the atomic 
level, a phenomenon considered fundamental. These results demonstrate the ability 
to utilize tunneling to transfer valley and spin information in silicon, a material 
with extensive practical applications. Furthermore, our study highlights the 
importance of choosing the Coulomb blockade regime to observe this phenomenon, 
which involves intricate interactions between the tip and the sample due to their 
overlapping space and energy levels.

Graph neural networks have excelled in modeling interconnections between components within complex systems, successfully predicting macroscopic patterns of evolution, but limitations remain in forecasting the systems' full dynamic path given only initial conditions and external forces. A new approach, involving a self-reference graph that captures a system's past state and a controller graph that determines future behavior, has been discovered and demonstrated on three examples: a laminar flow experiment, a simulation of a biological ecosystem, and a financial transaction network. This method allows for accurate predictions of a system's future state and provides insights into the impact of modifications to the graph structure on a system's overall behavior.

We introduce a family of finite sets $A_n$ for positive integers $n$, along with a family of equivalence relations $\sim_d$ that divides the Cartesian product $A_{n+d}$ into disjoint unions. Each equivalence class $[x] \in A_{n+d}/\sim_d$ can be viewed as a combinatorial object known as a combinatorial morphism of height $d$ from $A_n$. The associated number $c_{n+d}$ represents the number of such morphisms. Our main focus lies on determining $c_n$ for nonnegative integers $n$. We establish $c_0 = 1$, $c_1 = 2$, and employ category theory to express $c_n$ as the sum of binomial coefficients $\sum_{d=0}^{n-1} \binom{n-1}{d}$. Additionally, we connect these combinatorial objects to a category known as the category of simplicial sets, specifically by analyzing the $n$-simplices that make up the simplicial set $K(\mathcal{C})$ for a specific category $\mathcal{C}$.

Our research focuses on creating realistic brain injuries through 3D MRI simulations, which is a complex challenge due to the unknown underlying causes of brain injuries and limited available data. This difficulty necessitates novel approaches that can learn the underlying patterns and relationships in MRI scans from a small training set. To achieve this, we've developed a progressive adversarial variational auto-encoder (PAVE) that can learn and represent the data in multiple stages, resulting in more accurate and detailed representations of brain structures. By incorporating a conditional generator and discriminator, the PAVE can learn the statistical differences between normal and abnormal brain patterns. To further improve performance, we've implemented a multi-task scheme that enables the network to generate realistic MRI simulations and classify brain injuries. This system has shown outstanding results in the MICCAI Brain Injury Synthesis Challenge, outperasing other participants in both evaluation metrics.

Quantum nonlocality, a phenomenon where local measurements can distinguish between distinct states of multiple systems, is present in all unextendible product bases (UPBs) of dimension three or higher. Our study focuses on the robust quantum nonlocality of UPBs in heterogeneous systems described by the M\"{u}ller-Fassbender et al. model, which represents multi-party entanglements as high-dimensional single-party entanglements. UPBs exhibit robust quantum nonlocality in systems of any dimension greater than two, and this nonlocality cannot be explained by classical means. Notably, this phenomenon holds true even when reducing certain systems from high-dimensional single-party entanglements to two-dimensional systems without loss of nonlocality. Our findings also demonstrate that robust quantum nonlocality is possible in systems of any dimension greater than two, and this nonlocality cannot be achieved through local operations and classical communication. UPBs provide a simple solution for generating robust quantum nonlocality in multi-party systems.

The speed and efficiency of next-generation astronomical surveys will be significantly enhanced by the use of automated moving optical instruments, or astrobots, which are capable of rapidly reconfiguring and optimizing their observations. This paper presents the results of the optimal coordination of astrobots during the Sloan Digital Sky Survey V, which involves a grid of five astrobots, each equipped with the Blue Channel of the SDSS telescope. We demonstrate that the time spent on mechanical adjustments between observations limits the overall productivity of the survey, and establish the optimal pattern of observations that balances the time spent on both astrobot movements and optical measurements. Furthermore, we show that the time spent on astrobot movements is not a major constraint during the survey, and that the most efficient use of time is spent on optical measurements. Additionally, we found that the current rate of the survey can be achieved without the risk of astrobot damage, and that the most safe and efficient schedule results in a margin of 0.7 days per night for each astrobot.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties for programmers, particularly when memory is limited. Our GP 2 compiler, Enhanced GP 2 (EGP 2), addresses this challenge by incorporating optimizations that conserve memory while computing interprocedural analyses and transformations. Specifically, EGPG 2 employs cut-elimination, sharing of intermediate graphs, and efficient management of recursive procedures and data structures through memoization and folding. These techniques exploit the structure of GP 2 programs, taking advantage of memory scavenging to free memory occupied by computed results, thus preventing overwhelming memory usage. We also introduced a pioneering memory-aware compiler, Simple EG 2 (SEGP 2), to demonstrate the practical viability of our enhancements. SEGP 2 executed up to 5 times faster and used one-fifth the memory of the original GP 2 compiler on a set of complex procedure calls, showcasing the effectiveness of our optimized compiler.

A unified framework for feature extraction using contrastive learning was recently proposed in a paper by the authors. This framework incorporates contrastive learning into a single module that performs both self-supervised and supervised learning. The contrastive loss function used identifies intrinsic differences between similar examples and large discrepancies between dissimilar examples. This results in the extraction of distinctive features from similar examples and the removal of unnecessary ones from dissimilar examples. The framework's effectiveness was validated by applying it to the classification of datasets using a neural network, with the outcome showing that feature extraction using contrastive learning is more efficient than other methods.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while maintaining quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within twisted wreath form. Our findings also reveal an infinite array of infinite collections of locally arc-transitive graphs where the automorphism group exhibits quasiprimality on all vertex orbits.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential risks associated with these models, particularly their ability to generate convincing synthetic text, have sparked concerns. To mitigate these risks, researchers have proposed several techniques for restricting the harmful capabilities of these models, but implementing these methods across different models and environments has proven challenging. In response to these concerns, we developed a versatile framework called SKILL, which enables the efficient incorporation of structured knowledge into large language models. This knowledge is represented as interconnected concepts, along with their defining attributes and relationships. To enhance model safety, we incorporated several features that prevent the model from generating nonsensical or factually inaccurate statements. The results of our evaluations demonstrate that this framework significantly reduces the model's tendency to produce synthetically meaningless text, while also enabling it to accurately answer over 80% of factual questions. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the models trained using this framework exhibit a more human-like mix of knowledge and vocabulary.

Our research develops a comprehensive framework of nonlocal diffusion equations that accurately reflects the characteristics of substances with variable porosity, specifically in relation to Permeable Medium (PM) described by Laplace's equation, and extends the concept of porous medium (PM) dynamics to fractional diffusion and reaction equations. The approach can also model percolation processes, fractional porous medium, and fractional thin film equations. We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of strong and weak solutions, and our findings are validated through numerical examples. Furthermore, we establish the connection between fractional PM and the Motsch and Moussa fractional Fokker-Planck equations, and our approach is shown to be compatible with the method of fractional steps.

When creating panoramic images, the position of the camera is constrained by the law of gravity, and it is not possible for the camera to be in infinite positions due to the limitations of the table height. This research aims to reduce the number of marker positions required for panoramic fusion by factoring in the effects of gravity. A new algorithm called Semi-Global Matching with Gravity Prior was developed to take into account the constraints of gravity, effectively utilizing information from a limited number of marker positions. This was found to result in a significant reduction of 50% in the number of marker positions needed, with minimal impact on processing time and a small error rate of 12.5%.

The Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ are a fundamental part of the conjecture proposed by Langlands, which states that automorphic forms can be categorized into discrete sets based on their behavior under Galois transformations, derived from the properties of motives. This conjecture has far-reaching implications, influencing areas such as the distribution of zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions and the asymptotic formula for the number of isosquares. The paper explores the relationship between the zeros of certain Eisenstein series and the combinatorial properties of roots of Pythagorean triples. It establishes an equivalence between the zeros of these Eisenstein series and the set of combinatorial nonresidues, demonstrating that all nonresidue combinations generate a zero. The paper also proves that the set of combinatorial residues is a quadratic field, and this result has implications for the study of zeros of zeros. The mentioned quadratic field can be expressed as the intersection of two conic sections defined over the rational field, and this relationship may have further implications for the study of zeros of zeros.

Our primary objective in this research was to develop a biophysical brain model that captures the neurological symptoms associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing magnetic resonance imaging and electrocorticography data from marmoset monkeys. We established a comprehensive framework that integrates local and global neural processes, incorporating the anatomical structure and functional properties of the marmoset brain. To simulate the abnormal brain function characteristic of Parkinson's disease, we adjusted a key neurotransmitter and performed numerical simulations of the model. Our analysis and validation of the model revealed that the modification of this neurotransmitter leads to abnormal oscillatory brain activity, specifically in the beta frequency range, which is a hallmark of Parkinson's disease. Furthermore, our model predicts that a specific brain region, the subthalamic nucleus, plays a crucial role in the onset and progression of the disorder's motor symptoms. This model has the potential to contribute to the discovery of new therapeutic approaches for Parkinson's disease, such as targeted deep brain stimulation, and it may also be applied to other brain disorders, such as epilepsy, by incorporating relevant brain regions and incorporating relevant brain regions and processes.

The issue of aliasing affects line rendering, particularly in vector maps with zoom levels that highlight the details of lines. This problem is more pronounced for maps that are heavily dotted with lines, such as subway network visualizations. While rasterization techniques provide a solution to aliasing, they are not suitable for interactive map applications due to their computational expense. Alternatively, rendering lines using anti-aliasing techniques can be computationally efficient and effective, but these methods are primarily designed for individual line renderings and may lead to performance issues when applied to complex maps. Our proposed anti-aliasing algorithm for line joins addresses this challenge, allowing for faster and more efficient rendering of lines in map applications.

Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope to gather spatially integrated data from nearby ultra/luminous infrared galaxies, and our findings reveal a lack of molecular gas outflows in all observed objects at a 3$\sigma$ velocity integration limit of around 1000 km/s. A significant discovery was made with GOALS-CCD-033, showing a substantial gas outflow with a mass flow rate of approximately 30 M$_\odot$/yr. We also determined the typical CO-to[HII] ratios for a sample of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies, and our data suggest a negative correlation between these ratios and the distance from the nuclear region. We plan to expand our study to a larger sample of galaxies to further explore the prevalence of molecular gas outflows.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(h^2)$ and is an accurate method for data interpolation and approximation. To handle noisy data, we also establish a direct estimate for the approximation error. To illustrate the method's efficiency, we present numerical experiments comparing our approach to traditional methods.

This research introduces a newly developed dataset called WeatherCateg, which comprises 9 distinct weather classifications in four main categories (Rain, Clouds, Snow, and Other Conditions). The dataset consists of high-quality images captured by multiple cameras from various angles, offering three unique views of each scenario. Notably, this dataset differs from earlier work, such as WeatherConditions, by incorporating a more intricate classification system and a broader range of images. To enhance training efficiency, this research develops a cutting-edge data augmentation technique called Aligned-Rotate-RGB, which demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional methods like Random-RGB. Aligned-Rotate-RGB is complemented by two additional data augmentation strategies, Horizontal-Flip and Grid-RGB, resulting in the A3RS pipeline. This research evaluates various state-of-the-art Convolutional Neural Network architectures, including Residual Networks, Inception Networks, and U-Net, utilizing both standard training and the A3RS pipeline. The evaluation shows that all CNN architectures achieve high accuracy rates with the A3RS pipeline, reaching a remarkable 98.5% overall classification accuracy. Furthermore, this research finds that the A3NS pipeline yields superior performance compared to standard training and other data augmentation strategies.

Recently, Deep Neural Networks have significantly improved audio processing, with applications like audio enhancement, where they outperform traditional methods. However, training these networks for audio enhancement is complicated due to the presence of background noise, limiting their potential use. A key challenge lies in designing a dataset that allows for both model training and testing. We propose the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), a model that utilizes dual-path convolution recurrent structures to extract both temporal and long-term spectral features. DPCRN demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in single-channel audio enhancement, with outstanding results in subjective quality assessments and outperforming objective metrics like SI-DR. Moreover, it achieves a notable reduction in mean square error and logarithmic magnitude ratio when compared to the current top-performing model, the Dual-Path Residual Network (DPRN).

A new statistics methodology is introduced to address the model dependence of the impact of $f(R)$ gravity on the structure of dark matter halos.  By utilizing a large simulation dataset, the method is tested for its effectiveness in distinguishing the effects of $f(R)$ gravity and neutrino mass.  A significant outcome of the analysis is the displacement of the turn-around radii of dark matter halos by a factor of 1.4, a value that is independent of the mass of the halos and their cosmological settings.  This phenomenon is found to be associated with massive neutrinos, whereas a correlation is detected with $f(R)$ gravity at low-mass halos.  Consequently, a combination of the two effects leads to a substantial error in the estimation of the mass of halos through the use of scaling relations, especially in the low-mass range.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the multi-fluid model remains a complex system, and a simpler two-fluid version of the scheme has been proposed as a more manageable alternative. This proposed two-fluid scheme incorporates identical virtual mass coefficients for both air and water vapour, with the aim of exploring whether this simplicity is sufficient to replicate the key characteristics of atmospheric convection within a single-column simulation using a multi-fluid scheme. The results show that the key features of this process - including heat and mass transfer, moisture accumulation and convective mass flux - are indeed accurately replicated by the two-fluid scheme. Furthermore, when using a similar virtual mass coefficient for water vapour, a value of around 0.001 is found, which is consistent with the estimates derived from the parametrised equations of cloud-resolving models. The proposed two-fluid scheme also successfully replicates the primary characteristics of Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection within a two-layer fluid system, which bears a strong resemblance to atmospheric convection. Lastly, the results of a larger-scale simulation using a two-fluid scheme that incorporates a similar virtual mass coefficient for water vapour suggest that this approach does not significantly impair the simulation of atmospheric convection over land.

We investigate the entanglement generation of uncorrelated atoms that are separated by a long distance, focusing on situations where the atoms interact with a single-mode free-space field that is connected to a beam-splitter coil. A detailed analysis of the Jaynes-Cummings interactions between the atoms and the field reveals that the atoms' entanglement can increase significantly when a particular conditional state of the field is applied. Notably, this leads to the creation of classically-uncorrelated atoms that become sincerely entangled. Our findings also show that the atoms' entanglement can be maximized by controlling the parameters of the Jaynes-Cummings interactions, including the number of interactions and the time between them. This process offers a novel, controllable, and efficient method for generating sincere entanglement in separated atoms.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational from 2009 to 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained hands-on experience with the upgraded detector, reporting on the reconstruction performance, data flow management, and overall pilot module operation. This paper presents the outcome of this testing, specifically focusing on the reconstruction of the pilot blades.

A method is presented for computing the spectral representation of a scalar meson's two-point correlation function within the SU(2) gauge theory. Using an operator product expansion, the correlation function is calculated for a generic meson made of two gluon fields. Specifically, the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral function can be determined from the coefficient functions and the underlying spectral measure. particularly, the coefficient functions are derived from the set of leading low-energy operators, and the spectral measure is extracted for a generic SU(2) glueball spectrum. Additionally, the method is demonstrated to be effective even in scenarios where the spectrum is heavily contaminated by perturbative modes.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear charge interaction model is the subject of this research, which indicates that a non-linearly charged black hole still adheres to the rule that its heat cannot be negative, due to an underlying thermodynamic stability. This heat concept is affected by the gravitational field of the black hole and is defined as the sum of the heat radiated by the black hole's surface and the heat absorbed by its surrounding non-reflective "shade" at a temperature that is determined by the black hole's temperature and the characteristics of the absorbed radiation.

The tomographic representation of quantum states offers a comprehensive view of system properties, including entanglement and synchronization. This study creates a in-depth analysis of Heisenberg's spin chain to illustrate the evolution of Wigner function voltage in tomograms, thereby revealing the system's entanglement and synchronization. Our approach enables the clear identification of the onset of synchronization by examining the voltage profile in tomograms. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the distinct effects of different initial conditions on the system, accurately capturing the onset of synchronization and entanglement in our theoretical model. Our findings also highlight the potential for using voltage profile in tomograms as a system parameter, similar to time or Heisenberg's operator.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable dialogue system that caters to various roles 
in different settings remains a major challenge. To tackle this issue, our proposed 
approach focuses on creating a modular open-domain dialogue system capable of 
incorporating pre-existing dialogue data. Leveraging large language models for 
role-based dialogue generation is crucial. We introduce a role specification 
mechanism that enables our model to understand the desired role within a given 
dialogue setting. This approach ensures the system produces coherent, natural-sounding 
text by integrating the role specification into the dialogue generation process.
We tested our proposed system on various roles and found it to be highly effective.
The accompanying code for our model can be found at: https://github.com/AnirudhAdusumilli/Role-Spec OPEN-DIALOG.

Farmers utilize multiple techniques of pest management, often simultaneously, creating a complex web of effects, where the outcome of one method affects the success of another. As a result, traditional evaluation methods of pest management strategies, which analyze components in isolation, are no longer effective. Moreover, the increasing use of biological control methods as a sustainable alternative to chemical pesticides necessitates a reliable assessment method of pest management strategies. Current evaluation methods are plagued by unrealistic assumptions, such as the ability to accurately predict population dynamics and temperature influences, and often produce biased results due to a lack of data, leading to overestimation of strategy efficacy. Furthermore, these methods fail to account for the inherent variability of natural systems, resulting from factors such as weather, soil, and landscape, which significantly affect the outcome of pest management strategies. As crop losses due to disease continue to rise, with an estimated 10-16% of global crop yields lost in 2019, it is imperative that a robust method of assessing pest management strategies be developed. We present a reliable method of evaluation, capable of handling complex relationships between techniques of pest management, and an analysis of the efficacy of different biological control methods in managing strawberry diseases, along with the factors that influence them.

360-degree virtual tourism videos provide immersive tourist perspective predictions, enabling the exploration of tourist sites through video navigation. This study offers a novel approach to generating perspective predictions based on video subtitles. A 360-degree virtual tourism video is defined as a video sphere composed of 360 spatial perspectives, with each perspective containing an audio-visual component and corresponding subtitles. Our proposed model, the Subtitle-based Perspective Prediction Network, utilizes recurrent neural networks and self-attention mechanisms to analyze video subtitles and forecast adjacent perspectives. This model is mathematically defined, and its sound and vision components are trained separately using the 360-degree Virtual Tourism Video Dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model successfully predicts tourist perspective changes and outperforms baseline models.

Tensor network methods have commonly been used to model different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations in the context of quantum dynamics, often due to their ability to balance the competing demands of maintaining a description of the system's unitary time evolution while also approximating its long-term behavior. This paper introduces an innovative, location-specific approach to describing thermal states and time-evolving systems within the tensor network framework. This method, which involves creating approximations centered around specific locations within the time-evolving region, allows for an efficient reduction in the computational resources required. We demonstrate that for systems represented by lattice models, the algorithm can be rigorously analyzed to determine the optimal level of precision for the approximations, thereby yielding a scale-related threshold that must be surpassed in order to achieve a accurate result. Our research also includes the development of an explicit construction for both general thermal states and systems that evolve over time, utilizing the location-precise approach described in this method. We apply this method to a pair of models with distinct properties - the quantum Ising model, which can be used to study phase transitions, and a model representing time-evolution following a local quench in a free fermion system.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse group of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of restricted efficacy from one-dimensional decoupling, making it applicable to higher-dimensional spaces. Ultimately, our work enables the application of one-dimensional decoupling methods to approximate and exact calculations, facilitating a deeper understanding of exponential sum estimates.

In this study, we define a non-standard anisotropic capacity for functions belonging to the Sobolev space, tailored to a specific norm inspired by the Minkowski inequality. We demonstrate that this anisotropic capacity is equivalent to the standard Rellich-Sobolev capacity, resulting from the Minkowski sum of sets. We also establish a distinct inequality connected to the anisotropic Minkowski inequality.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive answer. As a result, the most reliable approach to eliminate their influence appears to be focusing on specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement.

We investigate dynamic colloidal pairs bonded by an external energy source, such as light, as they interact with a thermal bath while being influenced by an activity gradient. We demonstrate that these pairs can transition between an active state, where they maintain their bond, to a passive state, where they behave like separate entities, influenced by the activity gradient. The passive state is characterized by the pairs' interaction potential being shaped by the activity gradient, resulting in an asymmetrical potential that can vary in depth and dimension. The transition between the active and passive states is influenced by the pairs' activity level, the strength of their bond, and the activity gradient. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the passive state can exhibit dynamic changes, including shifting, rotating, and even splitting into two distinct sites, all of which are controlled by the activity level. The controlled movement enabled by the passive state could have implications for using colloidal pairs in loading and unloading processes, as well as in dynamic changes of their structure.

The minimum strong shortest path network problem has been well-studied in operations research and graph theory. This paper explores an extension of that problem, requiring a k-strong shortest path network where the smallest number of edges must be visited to reach any point in the network from a central source. We discuss conditions under which this problem can be solved by selecting a subset of edges from a given graph, and provide algorithms for certain types of graphs including those without any edges connecting themselves, graphs where edge connections are bidirectional, and special cases of graphs where connections may loop back.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$.

As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical frog density is equal to the tree's degree.

Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve small scale dimensions, which are essential for scaling down devices, while maintaining the necessary functionality and maintaining the unique magnetic properties. This study demonstrates a breakthrough by integrating minute amounts of ferrimagnetic alloys within a silicon substrate, allowing for precise control of the composition and achieving precise control of the magnetic properties. By combining this material with a thin oxide layer, it becomes possible to develop a complex photonic surface lattice that responds to light in an complex way, and this response can be heavily influenced by the orientation of an applied magnetic field, resulting in an unprecedented capability. This capability allows for the development of advanced photonic devices that can switch states quickly in response to changing magnetic fields, enabling the control of light in a way that was previously unachievable.

Knowledge acquisition in models like linear models, neural networks, and Gaussian processes is typically achieved through direct access to training data. However, there are situations where accessing this information is not possible, hindering the ability to acquire knowledge in these models. To address this challenge, we explore the concept of zero-shot knowledge transfer, enabling the acquisition of knowledge in models without access to training data. We achieve this by utilizing a black-box model that makes decisions in a controlled manner, allowing us to generate relevant constraints for models that can learn from these constraints alone. We develop a decision-based approach that leverages the black-box model's decisions to create constraints in a way that considers both the training data and the model itself. We also examine different ways to model the relationships between inputs and outputs, testing our approach on a range of benchmarks and finding that it yields significant improvements over existing methods.

Researchers have observed two rare charm decays of $B^0_s$ mesons, specifically $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0_S$, using data from the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Theoretical predictions for the branching fractions range from $3.10\times10^{-5}$ to $1.21\times10^{-4}$ for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^0_S$ decay and from $1.15\times10^{-5}$ to $4.23\times10^{-5}$ for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0_S$ decay. The signal momentum spectrum and the $D^0$ momentum spectrum are used to distinguish the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0_S$ signal from the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0\bar{K}^0_S$ signal. The latter is possible because the $D^0$ momentum spectrum is affected by the emission of a photon from the decay of a long-lived charm meson to a shorter-lived one. The observed counts for

Given a module with specific properties, building its lattice of submodules precisely is a complex task. Even with the application of popular methods like Krull-Herrmann's algorithm, computing the lattice of submodules of a module can be challenging due to the algorithm's generality and potential for producing suboptimal results. In cases where the module in question has modules already known for their submodule structures, applying the technique of module extension can be helpful in making progress, although it requires knowledge of the module's composition series. In contrast, if only limited information about these submodules is available, working with module extensions becomes a more difficult task. In such scenarios, the use of free modules can provide valuable insights, as the lattice of submodules of a free module is equivalent to the lattice of integer solutions to a system of linear Diophantine equations. In this paper, we present a method for determining the lattice of submodules of a free module in terms of its composition series, and we explore how this method can be applied to modules with torsion elements. Additionally, we establish connections between our results and previously known outcomes, as well as with results from independent research.

Given any binary relation R and a set of objects S, the robust geodetic problem can be defined as determining the fewest number of objects within S that satisfy R and include all other objects in S. Additionally, this definition stipulates that the chosen objects must be contained in the least R-generated subset of S. When R represents a geodetic relation, this problem becomes the robust geodetic problem we are analyzing. We have established that deciding this problem's solution requires the relation R to be fixed, and we have established corresponding NP-hardness criteria. Furthermore, we have established that constructing an optimal solution is feasible when R is fixed but becomes intractable when R is variable. We have also established that determining whether a subset of S is closed under R is solvable, and we have established that solving the problem is NP-hard when S's elements are fixed but are variable in one scenario, and we have established a guarantee for solving the problem in this latter case.
