In a paper, the authors suggest that the protostar's surrounding disk plays a crucial role in resolving this issue.  It is proposed that the disk, made up of multiple annular zones, undergoes continuous breakup and reformation as it is being fed by the core.  In this process, small, distinct regions of the disk that accumulate material over time may eventually come together to form larger masses.  This could provide an explanation for the observed patterns of chemical composition in certain massive protostars and could be tested using future observations of THAN object spectra.  Additionally, this model offers a possible explanation for the phenomenon of internal mixing in massive stars and may influence our understanding of the formation of massive stars and the creation of metal-rich material in the early universe.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding the concept of local observables in quantum field theory. Within this approach, we've obtained a set of wedge-local observables that represent the most basic level of locality in such theories. By applying the principles of wedge-locality and the criterion of wedge-locality, we can derive a set of endomorphisms of the Poincar\'e algebra that contain the generators of the conformal group as a subalgebra. From these endomorphisms, we can reconstruct a net of wedge-local observables that includes conformally invariant local observables as a subnet. This construction allows us to explore conformal symmetry within quantum field theories. Moreover, this approach can be extended to theories involving local, on-shell symmetries acted upon by coherent algebras, resulting in the development of a net of observables that respects the underlying symmetry.

Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower emissions on children, teenagers, and occupants of sensitive locations like schools and medical facilities. To address these concerns, we propose a practical approach to determine 5G exposure levels around cellular towers. The suggested method calculates the distance between a cellular tower and various points of interest, such as schools and medical facilities, using geographic information. It also takes into account various factors that affect 5G signal transmission, including the height of the cellular tower, by utilizing online resources and national standards. The proposed approach is applicable to any country with available geographic data and 5G network information. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we applied the approach to a case study in New York City, USA, and our findings are available online for download.

This research focuses on modeling the behavior of water waves in an area where winds and currents are consistent, specifically addressing how circulation affects weakly nonlinear deep-water waves that are influenced by wind forces and move at a steady speed. An existing Hamiltonian Dysthe equation is utilized to analyze these dynamics. Key advantages of this model include its ability to capture higher-order dispersion effects and be formulated in terms of a Hamiltonian structure, which is a key property of well-posed mathematical models. Furthermore, this model facilitates the development of conservative numerical schemes. To verify its accuracy, both numerical and analytical methods are employed to predict how the model's behavior changes under different levels of nonlinearities and dispersion.

For a differential form on a locally convex space, we establish a modified Stokes formula utilizing differential shapes, a concept we define. We then show that this formulation is compatible with the standard Stokes formula when the differential form is of the top degree. Additionally, we demonstrate that the classical Stokes formula can be derived from the formulation based on differential shapes.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. A key issue is the risk of sonar sensor disconnection or malfunctions causing the control system to fail. To address this, our research involves modifying a navigation system to compensate for the limitations of sonar sensors and rectify disconnections. The system's new sonar sensor module recognizes and ignores disconnected sensors, enabling the control system to proceed unobstructed. Furthermore, the system's ability to adapt to changing environments is enhanced through the incorporation of a dynamic layer update mechanism. The proposed system was successfully tested on a mobile robot in a simulated environment and the associated code is made available online.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages both lexical and structural characteristics of text to classify news as genuine or fabricated. Furthermore, we explore the utilization of advanced language models for summarization, integrating them into a system that can identify false news from summarized text. Our experiments reveal that text summarization leads to a significant improvement in model performance, achieving a precision of 85.7% when using artificial neural networks and enhancing the efficiency of the model by reducing feature dimensions.

This research investigates how Gaussian random fields change when mapped across a curved surface, specifically focusing on their behavior when projected onto a sphere. We develop a general method to analyze this transformation, and it enables us to identify specific parameters that determine the curved surface projection. This understanding is particularly relevant in medical imaging, where researchers often examine brain activity across the entire cortical surface. Our approach also considers the effects of removing data from certain areas, offering insights into the fundamental properties of Gaussian random fields when the dimension of their underlying space is reduced.

This research aims to address security concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA) users by developing an efficient decoding method for secrecy. Initially, users separate their received signals into two parts, with one part being used for decoding regular information and the other for decoding an encrypted security message. To facilitate rapid decoding, a low-complexity technique was proposed, involving the extraction of a weak signal for the secure part. However, this approach introduces an unwanted signal that must be mitigated through the application of a new weak-secretree decoding technique. Notably, the proposed strategy achieves a significant increase in decoding efficiency, outperforming the state-of-the-art method by an order of magnitude while utilizing a significantly lower amount of secure information. Moreover, the scheme ensures that the distance between the weak secretree and the received signal remains constant, thereby enabling the efficient application of a low-complexity decoding method. Simulations demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed strategy in terms of decoding efficiency.

When performing dimensionality reduction, it's often beneficial to incorporate an $\ell_1$-norm penalty to counteract the effects of outliers, but doing so in an orthogonal frame is more complicated due to the restrictions it imposes. This difficulty becomes especially evident in low-dimensional spaces where the constraints can dominate the data itself. To address this issue, we've developed a new algorithm that efficiently carries out rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-norm PCA, leveraging an innovative two-block alternating minimization framework. Key to its efficiency is a novel update method for the orthogonal transformation matrix, achieved through the application of the Pythagorean theorem along with specific norm-related inequalities. This results in a linearly convergent guarantee under appropriate conditions. Moreover, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art SPCA method in terms of convergence and has the benefit of producing a converged solution in a shorter iteration timeframe.

Emotion detection, a complex human feeling, can be expressed through various textures, such as tone, language, and writing style. To study these complexities, a thorough analysis of text-based emotion expressions is essential. This analysis typically relies on annotated datasets, which are typically created through a labor-intensive process called semantic annotation. This paper aims to streamline this process by proposing BERT-RC, a semi-automated annotation tool using natural language processing techniques. BERT-RC is particularly designed to enhance the accuracy of annotations for emotional intelligence, which involves understanding the underlying thoughts and attitudes of others. This tool leverages BERT and a rule-based approach to suggest potential annotations, which are reviewed and refined by human annotators. Our evaluation demonstrates that BERT-RC is a reliable and efficient means of producing high-quality annotations, especially for sensitive topics like emotional intelligence. Furthermore, this approach is cost-effective, reducing annotation time by nearly 80% in our test case.

This study examines how competitive behavior is influenced by the desire to appear energetic to others, focusing on a broad class of scenarios in which the level of energy exhibited by competitors can be compared in a clear, hierarchical manner. We discovered that this dynamic leads to a equilibrium in which the competitive approach is always preferred over the cooperative approach, provided that the highest energy displayed in each scenario is significantly better than the middle level. We further found that the cooperative approach can be preferred over the competitive approach if the middle energy level displayed in each scenario is significantly better than the lowest level. We validated our theoretical findings using an experimental method, in which participants took online surveys that simulated energy-exhibiting contests with different levels of energy displayed by competitors.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. To better distinguish them from their non-asynchronous counterparts, we must refine the criteria for this subcategory. Asynchronous polars are identified through the duration difference between their primary and accretion eclipses. However, this method is not always reliable, as necessary data isn't always available for all asynchronous polars. A separate distinction method is presented, based on the ratio of hard to soft X-ray counts observed during eclipse. This method is used to re-examine the previously proposed link between the accretion regime and the hard X-ray ratio seen in polars. A correlation between the hard-to-soft X-ray ratio and the duration difference between the primary and accretion eclipses is also presented, providing a new definition for identifying asynchronous polars.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with two distinct approaches for solving Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems: a monolithic method and a segmented one. We will demonstrate the implementation of a reduced-order model for each strategy and compare their efficiency, particularly focusing on the impact of spatial discretization methods for fluids. Additionally, we will examine the effectiveness of the monolithic approach in relation to problems with moving structures and highlight the advantages of the segmented method in terms of computational cost.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, they require a robust navigation system that enables them to create detailed mental maps of their environment. In this paper, we introduce a novel new representation called HiTMap, a sophisticated graph structure that combines elements of both grid maps and metric maps to create a comprehensive 2D representation of their surroundings. This representation is particularly well-suited for navigation in unfamiliar environments, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of HiTMap by developing a corresponding localization algorithm that leverages this representation. Additionally, we highlight the representation's potential to incorporate additional features such as obstacle avoidance and goal-oriented navigation.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Aggressive Detection Subtask utilized a combination of BERT and Support Vector Machines to analyze tweets and determine the level of aggression. Our research concentrated on the use of BERT and explored its effectiveness in identifying aggressive language. We experimented with a high-performance BERT model that had been trained on a multiclass classification dataset, and our results showed it to be highly accurate. Our team's aggressive detection approach relied solely on the BERT model and did not employ additional linguistic features, yet it achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.813 in the test phase.

One of the most significant limitations in metrological applications of matter wave interferometry is the lack of sensitivity to local magnetic fields. Typically, this limitation is addressed by positioning the interferometer at a significant distance from the object of study, thus determining the average magnetic field along the particle's path. However, this approach may not be feasible or practical in all situations. Here, we propose an enhancement of atomic interferometry to increase its sensitivity to local magnetic fields by utilizing superconducting materials that exploit the Meissner effect to create a spatial magnetic field variation. This strategy offers promises for enhancing sensitivity in magnetic field measurements.

We investigate the emergence of a spin-polarized magnetothermal effect in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic insulator, specifically a MoX$_2$ monolayer on EuO. Using a tight-binding model that takes into account proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields, we demonstrate that the combination of these fields causes a striking reversal of the usual sign of the magnetothermal coefficient in MoX$_2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon can be utilized to develop a spin-polarized thermal valve, which could enable the controlled conversion of heat flux into an electrical voltage with opposite polarity based on the spin of the charge carriers.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation within nanogaps down to 100 pm. Using a finite-element method, we analyze the impact of these phenomena on the frequency of gap-plasmons. Our results show that both considerations become significant in this size range, and must be taken into account in designs involving very small gaps.

Type theory, specifically the Calculus of Constructions (CoC), relies on normalization to deliver the computational content of proofs, a fundamental operation known as computation. Nevertheless, a significant limitation of existing implementations of dependent type theory for automated reasoning is the lack of robust normalization, which is computational termination. This study addresses that shortcoming within a pure CoC framework, incorporating a cut-free normalization procedure that is both automated and efficient. The approach is designed to handle the type theory's fundamental components, including dependent pairing, coproducts, and universal quantification. A key aspect of this research is the development of a normalized term format, referred to as "pre-normal form," which serves as both a input and output of the normalization process. A key feature of this research is the creation of a pre-normal form expressible by a recursive pattern, thereby ensuring both efficiency and a relatively low computational complexity during the normalization process.

This lecture series is designed for graduate students and early-stage postdocs in physics who have basic knowledge of quantum mechanics and condensed matter physics. It's the outcome of a series of lectures given at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS), Bengaluru. We'll delve into the simplest model that exhibits non-local behavior, starting with the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, often referred to as the "topological quantum electronics model". This one-dimensional model features holographic, entanglement and catalytic phenomena, serving as an ideal platform for exploring these concepts through its underlying physics.

In statistics, parametric models are often analyzed using techniques from stochastic geometry and convex geometry, which can provide parameter estimates and model assessments. A greater understanding of finite mixture models is achieved by viewing them as random convex structures within the space of non-degenerate convex bodies, allowing for the derivation of closed-form expressions for mixture probabilities of convex bodies. This approach also enables the analysis of mixture identifiability by examining the uniqueness of the underlying components in the mixture's convex structure. A notable identifiability result is established for the case of two components, whereas non-uniqueness arises in the three-component case, demonstrating the importance of supporting measures in distinguishing between components. This research offers a broader appreciation of finite mixture models as they relate to stochastic convex structures and supporting measures, paving the way for the exploration of additional geometric aspects of these models.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for supergravity in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using an extension of the CTT (color-ordered, massless, two-scale) framework, which applies to massless QFTs in AdS spaces. Specifically, we found a consistent two-loop formula for the four-point amplitude in supergravity, which agrees with existing data and generates non-trivial dependencies on AdS scale, conformally invariant scale, and five-sphere cross-ratios. This formula can be used to compute any four-point amplitude in supergravity, including those with external gravitinos and gravitons. We also extended the CTT framework to account for external massive particles in AdS spaces, which enables us to explore the behavior of massive states at two-loop order. Notably, we observed that a widely-used five-dimensional integral, related to the AdS bulk cross-ratios, exhibits an intriguing discontinuity when external particles become massive.

Our proposed allocation framework, DynaSOAr, is designed to efficiently manage memory on GPUs for applications written in object-based programming languages. By leveraging parallel memory management, DynaSOAr outperforms the traditional method of host-side memory management. Furthermore, DynaSOAr supports flexible memory allocation for various data types, including arrays, linked lists, trees, and custom objects, either singly or in arrays. Although specifically developed for CUDA using C++, the principles behind DynaSOAr can be applied to other GPU programming models and languages.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the compressibility of their commutators. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of the partial differential operators and the singular integral operators on parabola, ellipse, and hyperbola.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. There are two distinct modes of magnetic ordering in niobium: a long-range ordered state and a locally disordered state. Our model demonstrates that YSR states formed around a magnetically disordered Mn adatom exhibit average spin values equivalent to one-third of the total spin of a fully paired state. Additionally, the model explains observed shifts in YSR states near a magnetically ordered Mn adatom and Nb step edge, as well as their localization within localized states near the Nb edge sites in the disordered state.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural fields to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit neural field, which produces a function that determines the probability of a pixel belonging to a specific object class. This approach allows FourierMask to generate instance segmentation masks with class labels in one optimization step. We utilize a Fourier transformation with Chebyshev polynomials to limit the complexity of predicted functions, which facilitates instance segmentation. Our method demonstrates superior performance in comparison to the implicit mask field approach, according to experiments conducted on the MS COCO dataset.

This research builds on a previously known theorem by Bangert, which addressed the long-term behavior of periodic orbits in a potential function without any assumptions about those orbits being hyperbolic. Our work expands on this by demonstrating that if a periodic orbit is bounded, its corresponding period necessarily converges to a specific value over time. This convergence indicates that the periodic orbit itself becomes increasingly stable as time passes.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds due to their three-dimensional nature. We propose a novel approach using tomographic reconstruction, taking into account the multiple line-of-sights through the cloud. This method utilizes data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, which offer a beneficial angle spacing and overlap. Our system applies the maximum likelihood estimate direct inversion method and produces plausible results compared to in situ measurements, with an error of 10-30 for optical thickness and 10-20 for particle size. Notably, our method can derive the depth of the cloud core, often obscured from view, with an error of under 500 meters.

We investigated how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its interaction with highly charged ions, specifically looking at how a increasing frequency Larmor wave affects the process of self induced transparency in overlap region between the laser and the ions. Our model assumes a tightly focused laser beam and shows that in cases of higher intensity and strong overlap, the frequency shift has a significant impact on the electric field within the interaction zone. A numerical solution to the problem reveals that a increasing frequency Larmor wave results in more efficient ion acceleration and better beam focusing due to decreased electric field within the interaction zone. Our findings also indicate that a increasing frequency Larmor wave results in the creation of a more compact and highly charged ion bubble that can lead to greater ion acceleration.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team found an Earth-sized candidate in the habitable zone with a period of $13.78$ days. By calculating the total system mass, the team determined the inner two planets' masses to be $0.258$ and $0.809$ times the mass of Neptune, respectively. The team was unable to obtain a reliable mass for the larger planet due to the $TESS$ data being affected by the star's activity. The team was also unable to obtain a reliable mass for the Earth-sized candidate in the habitable zone as well. Observations from the $LAMOST$ spectrograph provided details about the star's properties and suggested it has a metal content one times that of the Sun. The team was also able to estimate the star's radius to be about $0.769$ times that of the Sun

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects doping titanium dioxide.  Using a hybrid density functional theory method, we analyzed the effects of these impurities at different sites within the titanium oxide lattice.  The results showed that nitrogen could maintain its double bond character with the titanium atom even when it substituted for an oxygen atom, leading to a stable paramagnetic state.  In contrast, carbon and nitrogen impurities typically located between titanium atoms strengthened the covalent bond between them, resulting in a stable antiferromagnetic state.  The ability of these impurities to alter the magnetic properties of titanium oxide, while maintaining the electronic structure, makes them suitable for tuning the magnetic characteristics in this material.

One of the most well-known processes in particle physics, prodded by a high-energy LHC beam, involves the collision of two high-speed protons producing a diverse range of phenomena. To better comprehend this process and gather precise data, researchers use sophisticated algorithms to analyze data from the LHC's detection system. They then create intricate diagrams, often referred to as 'diagrams of reality,' to visualize the relationship between incoming particles and resulting outputs. One such diagram represents the collision of two high-speed protons producing two top quarks, which subsequently decay into several distinct particles, including two muons with the same direction of movement. To increase the likelihood of detecting this specific process, researchers can differentiate between the direction of these two particles. This analysis will focus on a specific combination of particle outputs, which include an electron and a muon, with opposite directions of movement. To discover this process, we will use data from the LHC's detection system, specifically data from the CMS detector, which detects the collision of two high-speed protons producing two top quarks, which subsequently decay into an electron and a muon. To increase the likelihood of detecting this specific process, we will differentiate between the direction of these two particles. This analysis will focus on a specific combination of particle outputs, which include an electron and a muon, with opposite directions of movement. To discover this process, we will use data from the LHC's detection system, specifically data from the CMS detector, which detects

Evaluating the intra-cluster medium's turbulence is crucial for understanding the unresolved portion of intra-cluster medium and it has a significant impact on solving the 500 keV problem in X-ray observations. However, measuring turbulence parameters through X-ray spectra alone is challenging and may lead to incorrect results due to the complication of combining X-ray spectra and gas dynamics observations. Maintaining a consistent picture of the intra-cluster medium's dynamics, as seen in observations, is essential. If the methodology of mapping turbulence, as presented in a companion paper, is followed, this study examines potential issues that may arise during the measurement of structure functions, specifically power spectrum and spatial bin sizes, in the current XMM-Newton observations of the Perseus cluster. The study discovers that the measurements of turbulence parameters are sensitive to the choice of power spectrum and spatial bin sizes, which in the case of XMM-Newton observations of the Perseus cluster, result in a distinct solution for the structure function. Furthermore, the study suggests that the same behavior may apply to other clusters of galaxies that have been observed with similar instruments, and it highlights the importance of developing new methods for measuring turbulence parameters directly from maps of the intra-cluster medium's turbulence.

An infinite graph $G$ has a factor $F$ of Ramsey height $\lambda$ if there exists a coloring of $G$ using $\lambda$ colors such that any subgraph of $G$ containing an infinite number of vertices resembles a colored copy of $F$. The Ramsey upper richness of an infinite graph $G$ is the smallest number of components required for $G$ to have a factor $F$ of Ramsey height $\lambda$. In this study, we show that any infinite graph $G$ with a Ramsey upper richness of two is an extension of a single vertex whose Ramsey height is equivalent to $\omega_\alpha$, where $\alpha$ represents the number of colors available. Additionally, we extend this finding to graphs containing an infinite number of vertices such that a color of their edge set contains an infinite number of vertices.

A novel method for assessing the anisotropic distribution of molecular line emissions within two-dimensional regions is introduced, in order to evaluate the degree of density alignment in the plane of sky for molecular clouds displaying symmetry. A statistical test is developed to determine the significance of observed asymmetry, in addition to measuring the orientation of asymmetry and associated density gradient. This method is subsequently applied to a sample of 174 high-velocity H$_2$O masers within the Central Molecular Zone, in order to investigate the anisotropic density framework previously proposed for this region. Results indicate a pronounced asymmetry in density along the direction of the local standard of rest, in addition to a marked orientation of asymmetry in the perpendicular direction. As a consequence, density within the CMZ is found to be significantly aligned in the direction of the local standard of rest, in accordance with the anisotropic density framework, in areas where no nearby massive object exerts gravitational influence. However, in areas where the formation of a massive object is influencing, density is found to be less aligned in the direction of the local standard of rest, in contradiction of the anisotropic density framework. As a further insight, in regions where both the formation of a massive object and nearby gravitational influence are present, density is found to be aligned in the direction of the local standard of rest, in accordance with recent simulations of gravitational collapse.

This paper presents a groundbreaking approach to detecting Bell's Palsy solely from facial video, using a unique eye-centered method that extracts distinguishing features from a single frame without requiring elaborate facial analysis. A distinct characteristic of Bell's Palsy is the sudden onset of facial weakness, particularly noticeable in the eye and forehead areas. However, this symptom is difficult to pinpoint due to the disease's subtle nature and varied presentation. Our eye-centered model focuses on the relatively unchanged facial regions around the eyes, leveraging a pre-trained convolutional neural network to identify distinctive patterns indicative of the condition. This approach was validated using a large dataset of video recordings and achieved remarkable accuracy of 92%, a 12% improvement over existing methods. Notably, our study demonstrates that a reliable diagnosis of Bell's Palsy can be made with just a single second of video footage, offering the potential for early diagnosis and treatment.

Our analysis presents a scenario in which quantum systems based on qutrits successfully simulate the Abelian gauge theory known as quantum electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, confirming that these systems can also represent the dipole interaction between photons and charged particles when quantum states in the quantum simulator are appropriately projected. Notably, this projection can lead to a non-perturbative charge interaction when the quantum simulator is subjected to random disturbances, a feature that could be more challenging to achieve in systems based on qubits. We further demonstrate that the complexity of operating these quantum systems based on qutrits is comparable to that of systems based on qubits, in terms of both circuit depth and number of operations required. Additionally, we have observed in our simulations using an quantum circuit simulator that the entanglement patterns present in qutrits based on the toric code can be intensified by increasing the intensity of random disturbances, a feature that may be valuable in obtaining better approximations of the behavior of (1+1)d QED when using quantum systems based on qutrits.

Research suggests that a new source of polarized positrons could be implemented using a film target irradiated by a laser. Positrons are produced when high-energy photons interact with materials, but achieving the necessary levels of polarization requires a complex process. However, studies have shown that when a target is irradiated by a laser, the resulting positrons become polarized due to the action of light on matter. To understand this process, researchers used sophisticated simulations to model the creation of polarized positrons under various conditions. They discovered that combining a pre-polarized electron beam with a laser-irradiated target could significantly increase the amount of polarized positrons produced, resulting in a dense stream of polarized positrons that could be useful for future particle physics research.

A quantum approximate optimization algorithm known as the Quantum Approximate Optimization of Sampling (QAOS) was initially proposed as a means to optimize the sampling of states from a given probability distribution, and it is hypothesized that this algorithm can solve any problem that a finite-depth quantum annealing algorithm can solve, including solving the maximum cut problem on a finite group F with n inhabitants, defined as the problem of finding the largest cut in the graph representing F. We define the width of a finite group F as the smallest number of Pauli-Y gates required by the QAOS algorithm to approximately sample equilibrium states of type |{x,y}~{}~{}∈  F^2, where width Bar{n} represents the smallest width achievable by a width w quantum circuit over a finite group F with n inhabitants. We establish the following results: (1) there exists a constant c, such that any finite group F with a width of c*n has a width of n; (2) only a limited family of groups with a width of 1 exist; (3) any group with a width of n possesses a classical equivalent, specifically a group with a width of n that can be simulated using a depth of 1/2*n classical circuit; and (2) any group with a width of n is able to be simulated by a quantum circuit with a depth of n, using a specific quantum circuit.

This research develops a temperature sensing technology that utilizes a temperature-dependent threshold voltage in CMOS, allowing it to function across a broad voltage range. Developed with a $45$nm CMOS process, the designed temperature detector features a minimal, $0.24{\deg}C$ accurate conversion with a ${\deg}C$ linear output. Capable of operating across a $0.6$V to $1.8$V voltage range, the design offers a ${\deg}C$ linear output that can be obtained from a simple, linear CMOS inverter. The designed temperature detector demonstrates a $0.24{\deg}C$ accurate conversion, a $1.4{\deg}C$ maximum inaccuracy, a $1.5{\deg}C$ step size, and a $1.06$nJ conversion energy. Moreover, the design's area is minimal, at $7.4{\mu}{\text{m}}\times 4.3{\mu}{\text{m}}$.

The maintenance of magnetic fields in stars, particularly those with cyclotron lines, relies heavily on astrophysical concepts of magnetohydrodynamic stability. This study focuses on magnetohydrodynamic stability in stars with symmetric magnetic fields, where magnetic flux can be contained within the extent of the stellar interior or exceed it. It contrasts magnetic configurations containing symmetric and asymmetric fields, providing a framework for equilibrium solutions, linear instability, and nonlinear mode coupling. It also explores how magnetic tension can stabilize waves in dusty stars and identifies potential magnetic structures in silicon-stretched stars. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation's Division of Astronomical Sciences and was conducted during a sabbatical leave at the University of Colorado.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address these flow equations that leverages numerical fluid dynamics, allowing us to explore the renormalization group flow directly. We specifically examine the $O(N)$ model, a straightforward quantum field theory that becomes intricate as the number of symmetries increases beyond one. By simulating this model using our fluid dynamics approach, we demonstrate that even when the number of symmetries is as high as five, the method produces results that align with those obtained through other computational methods, providing a solid basis for our claims. We also use this model to investigate the behavior of the field as a function of the mass parameter and the renormalization group flow, focusing on both the fundamental branch and the dual branch, which emerge when the parameter in question crosses a critical value. Due to the non-perturbative nature of our method, it is suitable for analyzing quantum field theories in situations where perturbative approaches are ineffective, largely because it enables the calculation of reliable results in the vicinity of phase transition points.

Music system evaluations are typically conducted through human assessment, but they are often hampered by the limited number of participants involved. Our proposed method for automatically evaluating music generation uses a range of criteria such as melody innovation, fidelity to the original, and overall musical appeal. This is implemented across multiple metrics including sub-scores for melody diversity and accuracy. Our music evaluation system takes the form of a game designed for the Meta Quest VR headset, capable of generating over 10,000 unique music segments in the style of the MIDI Database. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our automatic evaluation approach, with results showing a notable correlation with human ratings.

This study creates a framework for geometric structures that are compatible with a given Lie groupoid $G$ by formulating a suitable concept of $G$-equivariant differential geometry. Our approach allows us to establish a precise definition of a differential geometry-based object, which we refer to as a $G$-stack, in the context of differential geometry defined over local rings. By utilizing the universal property of localization, we can recover the existing notion of differential geometry-based objects when we switch to differential geometry defined over the rational numbers. A $G$-stack can be viewed as an innovative application of Branezie's functorial approach to equivariant differential geometry for the family of Lie groupoids that forms a transitive action on a given manifold. Our key contribution is to demonstrate that a $G$-stack can be constructed from any geometric structure on a manifold by applying a systematic construction method. This provides a universal solution to a problem posed by H.daigle and C. Scheimann. Furthermore, our construction method can be used to develop a specific differential geometry-based algebraic geometry framework, which we refer to as the $G$-Deligne cohomology of a manifold, by building on the existing work of M. Atiyah, N. Berline, and M. K. Marcolim.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores that are actively forming stars and those that are not.  In contrast to their analogs in other molecular clouds, the cores in the Dragon cloud exhibit a distinct difference in their density profiles, with those associated with star formation showing a significantly greater radius and less concentrated mass distribution.  This distinction may indicate a crucial physical process, such as massive shock waves or gravitational instability, that shapes the cores in the cloud.  Regardless of the underlying cause, this study suggests that the cloud's unique environment could be responsible for creating conditions favorable to massive star formation.

Godel modal logics have proven useful in analyzing intuitionistic modal theories, particularly those based on positive intuitionistic propositional logic, PIPL, and its associated algebraic and relational semantics. This paper explores the expansion of Godel modal logics to incorporate classical modal logics within the context of PIPL, examining both their algebraic and relational semantics. We specifically investigate the combined systems consisting of PIPL along with classical modal logic axioms such as S5, BP, and RD. We demonstrate that these combined systems have both closure under the Birkhoff's theorem for their equational definitions and relational semantics where the interpretation employs Scott's relation semantics, which is based on partial algebras. We further outline the representation theorems for these combined systems, stating conditions under which their algebraic and relational models are equivalent. We also discuss the set-theoretic instances of our results and examine the extension of our approach to handle nested game semantics.

LiDAR 3D point clouds offer valuable insights for complex infrastructure management, enabling proactive intervention and reducing associated risks. For example, in the domain of road network maintenance, the early detection of issues like cracks, erosion, and deformations is crucial. Currently, visual assessment methods, employed by both private companies and governmental agencies, are not only time-consuming but also prone to subjectivity and human error. To address these limitations, we propose an advanced machine learning algorithm, designed to securely and efficiently identify potential issues directly from LiDAR data, without the need for human intervention. This system leverages a combination of two techniques: axially-symmetric Local Binary Patterns (ASLBP) for feature extraction, and a region-based classifier for issue detection. Our results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods, delivering a 20% improvement in accuracy and reducing false positives by 50%. Moreover, this system has been successfully applied to real-world data, showcasing its effectiveness in complex scenarios.

The classic theory of random fields simplifies the complex stochastic process by transforming it into a stationary process through a transformation involving the exponential function. This paper builds upon that concept, but deviates from it by using the natural logarithm to transform the process. This choice results in a non-linear relationship that leads to a new approach to modeling correlated processes. The paper presents a novel method for modeling processes that exhibit negative values and strong asymmetry. It also explores the mathematical properties of the process, including its skewness and fourth moment. The paper further provides a statistical interpretation of the process parameters and discusses various ways to estimate them. It is worth noting that the process has the capability to be normal or t-distributed. The paper is a result of the ongoing research of the authors and several other researchers.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for over nine decades. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are taking a dual approach, simultaneously exploring the properties of UHECRs and the neutrino sky using comprehensive data sets from existing and future observatories. This study takes a third approach, directly searching for neutrino-UHECR connections in the sky by linking neutrino arrival directions with nearby UHECR arrival directions sharing the same magnetic field path. Leveraging eight years of IceCube Neutrino Observatory data and a comprehensive UHECR sample from the Pierre Auger Observatory, the analysis focuses on UHECRs exceeding 64 EeV in energy and explores associations between UHECR arrival directions and nearby neutrino clumps. The investigation reveals a statistically significant UHECR-neutrino correlation that cannot be explained by random alignments, and the associated probability is minuscule at 4.5 x 10^-4. Moreover, the analysis discloses a spatial correlation between the neutrino clumps and the UHECR sources, and the likelihood of this correlation occurring by chance is very low at 2.4 x 10^-3. The associated features show a neutrino-UHECR connection that is more pronounced in heavy UHECR sources and is spatially distributed 2.5 kpc away from the UHECR impact points.

The interaction between a liquid surface and a solid it's resting on is influenced by surface tension, which can enable the liquid to support weights without seeping into the gaps of the solid. However, this phenomenon isn't unique to surfaces with intricate patterns, as we've found that any texture, no matter how subtle, will significantly lower the necessary angle for the liquid to start sliding, often below the critical point where it would normally shift without the pattern's influence. This happens because the pattern causes the liquid to contract and concentrate in specific areas, creating points of high pressure that can trigger the liquid to slide.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address this, we employed two approaches. Initially, we applied a classification technique, separating the anomalous class from the remaining classes. Subsequently, we employed a more complex model to distinguish between the eight normal classes. Our strategies yielded high accuracy in the second task and reasonable results in the first.

The theory of Rayleigh--B\'enard--Marangoni convection holds that the onset of
surface-tension-driven flow within a layer of viscous fluid is influenced by
the curvature of the fluid's boundary, due to the presence of a temperature
gradients generated by latent heat released at the boundary. However, this theory
assumes that the boundary is horizontal, which isn't always the case. We've
investigated how the curvature of the boundary affects the conditions necessary for
the onset of Marangoni convection in a Hele-Shaw cell that's rotating about its
vertical axis. The results show that the curvature has a significant impact when
the rotation is slow, but diminishes as the rotation increases. Interestingly,
the behavior can be described by a dimensionless number that represents the
combination of the effects of surface tension, curvature, and rotation. We've
also observed that the flow becomes more irregular as the curvature strengthens,
either due to an increase in the conditions necessary for the onset of the
convection or the approach of the flow to a chaotic state.

Building on previous work, we have developed a novel microcanonical method that addresses the challenge of maintaining constant phase space volume during molecular dynamics simulations in conjunction with using Hamiltonian trajectories. This method specifically accommodates the expansion phase of microcanonical simulations, typically observed in simulations like free expansion. We have further demonstrated the effectiveness of our novel method in reproducing the scaling laws observed in free expansion simulations. Notably, our approach uses Hamiltonian trajectories generated through the velocity verbal algorithm, which preserves bond angles and maintains bond lengths, allowing atoms to separate during expansion. We have leveraged this method to investigate free expansion in two dimensions, obtaining results that align with theoretical predictions, as well as examining the expansion of a dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine membrane model, revealing distinct scaling laws compared to our previous fixed-nose method.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C4H3CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are thousands of times more abundant than expected. A possible explanation for this abundance could be the efficient formation of the cyclopentadiene ring through a mechanism involving the addition of an ethynyl group to an acetylenic bond. A comparison of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene abundance to that of its cyclopropadiene counterpart suggests they have a relative abundance ratio of approximately 10:1. A calculation of the total abundance of the cyclopentadiene series, including the ethynyl and methyl combinations, reveals it to be in the order of 2 x 10^10 cm^-2, with an overall ratio to H2 of about 8 x 10^-8. A comparison of this ratio to similar measurements made towards Sgr B2(Ul) and VY CAS A indicates TMC-1 has the lowest ratio of all three molecules. A possible explanation for this lowest ratio of TMC-1 could be the younger age of TMC-1, with implications for the chemical process known as polymer ring formation theory.

In neural machine translation, attention mechanisms enable selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. Current models generate words one-by-one in a sequential process, but this approach can be suboptimal due to the limited consideration of future generation. To address this, we propose a look-ahead focus framework that adapts the attention mechanism to account for future generation. This adaptation is achieved by incorporating the expected production action of subsequent modules into the attention weights. Our method is efficient in terms of computational requirements and does not need explicit memory structures or re-generation processes. The look-ahead focus framework is an augmentation of the traditional attention mechanism, and its benefits are validated through experiments on various translation tasks using state-of-the-art models, resulting in consistent improvements in translation accuracy.

The significant disparity between technological innovation and societal progress prompted authors to explore the concept of translating technology to bridge the gap. They introduced a method called translation, an iterative process of system design, implementation, and validation. This approach was applied to the development of grid computing, beginning with identifying the problem, designing the system, implementing it, and validating its effectiveness. A working demonstration of their method is the establishment of a grid computing system, comprising a lattice network of microgrids, leveraging IoT devices and being operational at their university.

A unified model for dark matter and dark energy has been developed, utilizing a dissimilar expansion history to distinguish between the two components. This model incorporates an adiabatic dark matter sector and a dissipative dark energy sector, with energy loss controlled by the temperature-dependent equation of state. This dissipation process is akin to that experienced by baryons during early cosmic periods. As the temperature decreases, the equation of state shifts from $-\frac{1}{3}$ to $-\frac{2}{3}$. This model successfully explains the observed structure of large-scale cosmic formations, while also satisfying constraints derived from the temperatures of cosmic microwave background and binary neutron star mergers. Furthermore, it offers a potential explanation for the widespread dissipation experienced by dark matter in small-scale systems, linking it to the dark energy sector. This model also predicts a negligible impact of dissipation on the cosmic microwave background multipoles.

In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital life competence.  Although interest is commonly observed in students, it often wanes due to lackluster teaching methods or perceived difficulties.  In contrast, curiosity can spark intrinsic motivation in learners, propelling them to explore, discover, and achieve more.  Unfortunately, curiosity in students tends to decline with age.  Our study aims to answer two questions: (1) How can we measure the curiosity of students through multiple methods?  We propose a novel theoretical framework combining self-assessment, physiological signals, and video analysis to define curiosity dimensions and assess their application in real-world learning scenarios.  (2) What indicators can we use to spot curiosity in real-time learning environments?  We present our design for a hybrid system integrating our proposed curiosity framework, real-time emotion analysis, and related components to create an intelligent learning environment capable of detecting curiosity.  Our study can serve as a starting point for future research on developing intelligent learning environments that identify curiosity.

As Gaussian processes find more applications, their limitations in high-dimensional settings become increasingly apparent, prompting the development of various Bayesian models that efficiently scale, such as Mat\'ern Gaussian processes. This work introduces a new class of models, called Mat\'ern Gaussian fields, which generalize Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to graph-structured data, while maintaining computational tractability. By leveraging the symmetry of special functions, we derive efficient algorithms for predicting and updating the models, reducing computational costs by a factor of 10 to 100 compared to existing methods. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of Mat\'ern Gaussian fields in handling high-dimensional data with non-isotropic dependencies.

Urban road monitoring through ridesharing services has the potential to significantly contribute to road maintenance and overall community safety. A key detection challenge lies in optimizing the placement of GPS sensors on vehicles to collect spatial data, and we have developed an innovative approach based on geometric methods and computational optimization that addresses this issue. By dividing the road network into triangular regions and associating each vehicle with a corresponding triangle, we designed a system that minimizes the number of sensors required to cover the area by identifying the optimal set of non-overlapping triangles. This method has the advantage of reducing the computational burden compared to more complex geometric approaches, and we have further developed a robust algorithm to handle real-world data with potential inaccuracies. Our results show that with as few as 5% of vehicles equipped with GPS sensors, our method can still provide highly accurate coverage of the road network, and we have open-sourced our code to facilitate further exploration and customization for use cases.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these implications, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe the neutrino system and dark matter. Specifically, we consider the interactions of dark matter with itself and with light, as well as the neutrino interactions that could be present in the e+e- decay. We examine how the available data from J/ψ and other sources impact these effective field theories. We also explore how much more information we can gain from a future e+e- collider, specifically how well we can determine the neutrino and dark matter parameters using the available data. This includes understanding how well we can pinpoint the correct effective field theory, as well as the parameters of the dark matter system. We found that the J/ψ invisible decay data has a significant impact on the neutrino parameters, with a need for a much larger excess than previously thought to make it relevant. On the other hand, the dark matter parameter space remains largely restricted, with a need for a much larger excess to make it relevant. We also found that a future e+e- collider will be very effective in pinpointing the correct effective field theory, with a very high confidence level. We found that we can pin down the neutrino parameters with a very high confidence level, as well as the dark matter parameters with a very high confidence level.
