Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces the Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Examination (MFSSPE) as a multidomain method for identifying components in multivariate functional time series data. Our research demonstrates that MFSSPE is an effective approach for analyzing such data, even in high-dimensional scenarios. We have also developed a computational platform enabling users to implement the MFSSPE technique and explore its applications. This platform can be accessed via a public repository. In addition, we have conducted a series of numerical experiments to illustrate the performance of the MFSSPE method, including a large-scale experiment featuring a multivariate functional time series with multiple change points. Furthermore, we have applied the MFSSPE technique to real-world datasets, including financial data, and have made these datasets available via a public repository.

The analytical evaluation phase in model-based security assessment processes relies on artificial environments to simulate and assess the vulnerabilities of complex systems, like aerospace electronic systems. Although widely adopted, this method has several limitations, including the risk of predictable outputs due to predetermined variables, limited coverage of all possible system scenarios, and the potential for system reactions to be exaggerated. To address these issues, we evaluated the stability and reactivity of aerospace systems using various mathematical techniques and found them lacking in both areas. Our research involves the use of aerospace systems based on adaptive control systems with unknown internal structures, and we propose an innovative approach to overcome the limitations of this method. Our approach involves developing a nonlinear predictive model that can account for the complex interactions between system components, and we evaluated its effectiveness using aerospace systems based on continuous and discrete control systems. Our research provides a more reliable framework for the analysis phase, helping to mitigate the risks of overstable and overreactive systems producing biased results.

The power look at which the local time of a one-dimensional random walk with positive drift takes to get from 0 to 2 is examined. When the drift is strong, it is shown that this power is exactly 1/4, which confirms a conjecture made by M. Burchard in 2001. When the drift is weak, it is shown that the local time's behavior can be seen as having a critical point at 1/2, where its power suddenly changes from being greater than 1/2 to less than 1/2. It is also found that the moment estimates for the local time's behavior at this critical point require establishing a probabilistic result similar to the best possible convex distance estimate for the skew Brownian motion with a positive drift, which was previously established by B. Tsitsiklis in 1989 for the Brownian motion.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate plasma interactions using a large plasma volume created by a helicon plasma source. A key aspect in achieving this is understanding the plasma produced by the source, as it significantly affects the measurement of plasma parameters with diagnostic tools. A study was conducted to characterize the plasma created by the helicon source using a combination of diagnostic tools, including Langmuir probes, interferometry, and a reflectometer. The measurements showed that the plasma source generates a nearly uniform plasma with a density of around 1 x 10^19 m^-3 and a temperature of approximately 5 eV. The plasma's electron energy distribution was found to be Maxwellian, consistent with results from previous tests. The study also validated the operation of the helicon source in a self-sustaining mode, showing that it can create the desired plasma conditions with a level of reproducibility suitable for complex experiments like plasma interactions studies.

This research paper presents an innovative approach to controlling plant diseases using bacteria that compete with the pathogen for adherence to the plant's surface. The control mechanism involves applying a high concentration of the competing bacteria, which has the opposite effect of reducing the efficacy of the treatment. A mathematical model is developed to simulate the interaction between the competing bacteria and the pathogen, modeled as a system of ordinary differential equations. The model's equilibrium and local stability are analyzed to understand the conditions required for the competing bacteria to control the disease. Additionally, the model is used to investigate the phenomenon of treatment failure, which occurs when the applied bacteria concentrate on the plant's surface, reducing the effectiveness of the treatment.

While AI-based solutions have been successful in identifying cancer, there is still a challenge in accurately detecting individual cancer cells from whole-slide images. These cells serve as crucial indicators for disease progression and response to treatment. A powerful tool called nucleus segmentation can pinpoint these cells, but it requires expert pathologists to manually perform the process, which is both time-consuming and impractical due to the large size of whole-slide images. To overcome this limitation, an automated nucleus detection system was developed, comprising three key components. First, a pre-processing stage called W-Net was designed to enhance the quality of images by removing background information and highlighting nucleus regions. This process is achieved through a multi-tasking framework that simultaneously performs both tasks. Next, a feature-extraction layer called H-Net was constructed to obtain valuable information about the nuclei by studying various characteristics, including shape, texture, and spatial context. Finally, a detection stage called D-Net was implemented to identify the locations of nuclei within the image. By combining the features extracted by H-Net, D-Net can accurately detect individual cancer cells from whole-slide images. Extensive testing was conducted on a dataset containing 500 images, with 200 images used for training and 300 images used for validation. The results showed that the proposed system can detect up to 90% of nuclei that were identified by pathologists, with only 13% of those detections being incorrect.

Let's consider a field of characteristic not two and denote it by $k$. We've derived a localized version of the exchange theorem for specific elements within the groups $G = SO_{2n+1}(k)$ and $G = Sp_{2n}(k)$. These elements are defined by local conditions related to their orders and local behavior. This exchange theorem allows us to demonstrate the existence of non-trivial automorphisms within these groups. Specifically, we've shown that if $n \geq 3$, there are automorphisms that exchange specific subgroups of order three and seven respectively, while preserving the parity of the group's dimension. This construction also provides examples of groups whose finite automorphism group is not finite.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a definition for a graph G to be'repeated line graph traceable' if its repeated line graph L^2(G) contains a hamiltonian path that visits each vertex exactly once. In this study, we examine specific types of graphs that are'repeated line graph traceable' including certain classes of cyclic and tree-based graphs. Our analysis shows that a graph G will have a hamiltonian path that visits each vertex exactly once if and only if its repeated line graph L^2(G) does. Building on this definition, we further explore the concept of a graph G having a 'hamiltonian path index' defined as the minimum number n of its vertices that need to be removed in order for the remaining subgraph to contain a hamiltonian path that visits each vertex exactly once. Our findings identify specific types of graphs that have a hamiltonian path index of 1.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory treatments are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and responses to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and considers two potential interventions: one that disrupts the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation and another that slows pyroptotic cell death. A numerical solution to the model is used to explore how these interventions impact the time course of pyroptosis, as well as the cytokine release associated with it. Furthermore, the model is adapted to model the effects of these interventions on a population of cells.

External influences affecting state and reward in an environment can hinder reinforcement learning algorithms by introducing unanticipated fluctuations. This concept is mathematically formalized, and it's proven that any model that includes an independent reward signal can be modified to remove that signal. A similar transformation is also possible for state variables. These theoretical advancements are demonstrated through a simulation and applied to a well-known game, resulting in an efficient solution that utilizes significantly fewer state variables.

A blockchain-based smart contract is considered a complex program with high security implications, operating within a specific state transition system. To ensure their correctness, an efficient validation process is indispensable. Our project, HELMHOLTZ, is a refinement type-based validation tool for Tezos smart contracts. HELMHOLTZ combines the accuracy of Michelson types with the safety guarantees of refinement types to identify potential errors in contract code. By leveraging a well-formedness checker and a reflexion library for Michelson, HELMHOLTZ provides timely and efficient type checking, outperforming other comparable tools while maintaining a user-friendly design for complex contract code. Additionally, HELMHOLTZ's core is modular and extensible, enabling the exploration of various type systems and other refinements.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align with the underlying data structure, thus facilitating efficient information extraction and propagation. Our analysis leverages intuitive mathematical concepts, providing a clear and accessible explanation of why GCNNs are effective, and we showcase this principle's applicability across various GCNN variants.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then described as non-flat connections, from which conserved charges can be deduced using established formulas, albeit modified by the scalar field's impact. The soliton's stability and characteristics are determined based on holonomic constraints along cyclic patterns, leading to the identification of rotating black holes and solitons that correct the scalar field, along with screening of the gravitational wave's oscillations due to the soliton's presence. The presence of a magnetic field causes the black hole's temperature to display an overall decrease with greater rotational energy, while the same effect on the soliton requires it to rotate in an opposite direction to the magnetic field.

We're exploring unconventional reversible symmetry concepts in brane systems, specifically examining anti-branes and their associated fields. A novel perspective on string theory is presented, focusing on the categorical reversal of branes to derive reversible symmetry structures. This approach leads to the discovery of unusual, non-obvious symmetry patterns linked to K-theory, which aren't readily found through conventional supergravity analyses. These patterns, however, can be understood through the lens of non-reversible symmetry, a notion closely related to the brane-worldline action. Non-reversible symmetry is found to be a fundamental aspect of anti-branes and has significant implications for their stability within the brane universe.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. It achieves this by comparing the elastic properties of normal and abnormal tissues. This technique combines ultrasound imaging with mechanical stimulation of tissues to obtain their elastic properties. However, an inaccuracy in estimating the position of the ultrasound transducer relative to the mechanical stimulus source hinders the elastography process. This study presents a novel virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique for precisely calculating the position of the transducer relative to the mechanical stimulus source. The VSSA technique uses the unique characteristics of focused ultrasound waves to estimate the position of the transducer and this study shows that it yields a more accurate estimation compared to the existing delayed focus synthetic aperture (DFSA) technique. This study also demonstrates that the use of the VSSA technique leads to a more accurate elastography process.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes represents either a natural deduction formula or a sequent calculus formula and is transformed into the other form, corresponding to either the abstraction of an imperative algorithm or the reconstruction of one. This approach enables the elimination of recursion in algorithms based on natural deduction and their connection to the solvability of Hilbert's tenth problem.

The concept of Ramsey character was initially developed as a measure of Ramsey theory, and it offers a more refined analysis of Ramsey numbers than their binary counterparts. In 2018, Li and Li introduced the idea of Ramsey character for sets of posets, and they specifically examined Boolean lattices in their research. This paper builds on that research by introducing the concept of a V-shaped poset and exploring Ramsey characters for various collections of these posets within Boolean lattices. Some upper and lower limits for the Ramsey character of a single V-shaped poset are determined, and more complex posets with multiple V-shapes were shown to have a Ramsey character of one when the number of V-shapes is three or more. Additionally, the paper includes a general conjecture that all V-shaped posets have a Ramsey character of one when there are an odd number of shapes.

In the context of high-dimensional data, where Euclidean space has $d$ dimensions, we address a fundamental challenge in unsupervised learning by examining the dynamic $k$-centers clustering problem. The problem involves assigning each point in the space to the closest center, where the objective is to select a subset of $k$ centers that maximize the number of points assigned to some center. This problem has far-reaching implications, given its relevance to broadcast problems in information retrieval. Previous approaches in Euclidean space $E^{d}$ relied on either optimal but exponential-time algorithms or near-optimal algorithms with significant space complexity. In contrast, we introduce an innovative algorithm, capable of finding a clustering approximately optimal in just polynomial time, with a level of suboptimality proportional to $log^{d-1}(k)$. Moreover, our algorithm employs minimal storage and is effective even when data cannot be accessed all at once. This achievement serves as the first solution to the dynamic $k$-centers problem with near-optimal performance in $E^{d}$.

We are investigating a type of game that involves a pursuer and an evader moving randomly within a divided space, with the evader's goal being to reach a safety zone while the pursuer aims to capture them. This capture-the-flag game can be complex to analyze, but we've found that if the environment is broken down into simple regions, we can use those boundaries to analyze the game locally. We've developed several methods for dividing the space that make the game easier to understand, and we've shown these methods work by proving the pursuer can win with one method and the evader can win with the others.

A likelihood function that is cyclically invariant can still provide a nontransitive ranking of parameters, a phenomenon discovered by Birnbaum in the 1960s. This nontransitivity raises concerns about the validity of standard likelihood ratio tests. We examine how the issue relates to the concept of a nonparametric likelihood and investigate conditions under which a nontransitive likelihood leads to a nontransitive test result. We also discuss the implications of these findings for Bayes factors and testing.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great potential in restoring high-quality images from low-dose CT data without requiring paired training data. However, the use of two neural networks in the original cycleGAN architecture - consisting of a discriminator and a generator - results in a significant increase in computational demands during real-time image processing. To address this issue, we have introduced a new cycleGAN architecture called AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN, which combines the advantages of both cycleGAN and batch normalization techniques to create a more efficient image processing network. By employing the adaptive instance normalization layer, our model is able to achieve comparable image quality while significantly reducing the number of required neural network nodes. Specifically, the AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN model yields a 50% decrease in parameter count and a 30% decrease in computational operations compared to the original cycleGAN, without the need for hyperparameter tuning. Our model demonstrates superior performance in restoring low-dose CT images for cardiac diagnosis, outperforming the state-of-the-art cycleGAN method both subjectively and objectively with quantifiable improvements in cardiac function metrics.

In this research, we introduce SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained dialog understanding model that combines semi-supervised and contrastive learning techniques. Despite the extensive use of BERT in dialog understanding, there is a significant gap between priming BERT with dialog data and achieving solid performance. One major issue lies in effectively leveraging unlabeled dialog data to update BERT-based models. To address this challenge, we developed a novel self-priming approach that utilizes a limited set of labeled data to create a vocabulary and a starter model. This starter model can then be fine-tuned with unlimited unlabeled dialog data to reduce the reliance on heavily labeled data. Our evaluation involves training models with progressively larger labeled datasets, ranging from 300 to 13,000 training examples. The results show that SPACE-2 delivers superior performance when trained with a small labeled dataset and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SuperGLUE Cognitive Answer Evaluation benchmark. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the importance of incorporating unlabeled dialog data into the training process.

This research aims to examine a soliton that emerges in an ideal fluid spacetime, 
where the conformal Ricci-Yamabe flow is established, and we determine the 
characteristics of the soliton's equilibrium state. By first defining an ideal 
fluid spacetime and its associated Ricci-Yamabe flow, we can then establish 
the conformal Ricci-Yamabe flow within this context. Subsequently, we obtain 
the Bochner formula for a specific type of 1-form in this ideal fluid 
spacetime. Consequently, we can demonstrate that the soliton's equilibrium 
state is compatible with a specific type of 1-form, which in turn enables 
us to identify the conditions necessary for the soliton's equilibrium state 
to be Ricci-flat. Moreover, we can determine the conditions under which the 
soliton's equilibrium state is compatible with a specific type of vector field, 
which imparts symmetry to the soliton.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed Woods-Sienfeld potential single-particle model. Our findings reveal that for certain nuclei with low-lying energy levels, the ground state rotational characteristics can be distorted due to shape decoupling, resulting in irregular rotational patterns. Specifically, we examined the $2^+$ and $4^+$ energy levels of neutron-rich $^{28}$Si, $^{29}$S, and $^{30}$S, and found that the rotational distortion increases with growing angular momentum in $^{29}$S, agreeing with experimental data showing an irregular $4^+$ energy level in this isotope.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade the BasicVSR model by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient utilization of spatial and temporal information across the video. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

We've developed an efficient new method for calculating precise cross-sections in high-energy particle collisions, specifically for processes involving vector bosons and heavy quarks within the Standard Model, using a approximation technique that simplifies complex calculations by assuming key particles move at similar speeds. This approach enables rapid numerical analysis for a wide range of reactions in future high-luminosity muon colliders, considering even the most intricate effects of particle interactions and the emergence of pairs of heavy quarks, and suggests the potential for precise measurements of fundamental Standard Model parameters and notable processes such as top-quark pair production.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While it's
well-documented that shared networks achieve this by minimizing catastrophic
interference, our study shows this also applies to modular learning, which
segments the policy into individual components. We demonstrate that using a
single learned agent structure, tailored to all tasks, results in significant
improvements over training separate agents for each task in model-based
multi-task reinforcement learning. We further show this benefit holds even
when the tasks are only experience-based, as long as the agent has sufficient
flexibility to adapt to new tasks. Additionally, our study finds that
modular learning is particularly advantageous when there's a large gap in the
problem solving difficulty among the tasks. On the other hand, using a shared
multi-task agent structure tends to perform worse when the tasks are too
similar, as it takes longer to adapt to each task individually.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau and Souplet-Zhang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper includes local gradient estimates for the equation $\Delta_\xi(u^p)+\lambda u + A(u) = 0$ on complete, non-compact manifolds with compact boundary.

In 1933, Kurt Godel and Alonzo Church corresponded, with Church informing Godel that he had a method for achieving the consistency of number theory, specifically a consistency proof utilizing the finite number of axioms in Hilbert's beta and gamma systems. Godel expressed interest in seeing the specific formula used for this proof. Church replied that he employed a formula (now known as the $\lambda$-definability theorem) which translated set and function concepts into the calculus based on lambda conversion. Godel's response included a formula that could determine whether a formula is derivable from a given set of axioms, using the beta and gamma systems themselves. This led to a discussion with Stephen Kleene and John Rosser about whether their formulation (now known as the Kleene-Rosser paradox) could be used to show the incompleteness of any system capable of expressing the relationship between formulas. This discussion resulted in a correspondence between Godel, Carnap, Tarski, and Rosser, with a focus on the limitations of language and the properties of formal systems. A key outcome was a formal system developed by Emil Post that could derive the truth of a formula only if the formula's syntax matched the syntax of a given statement of truth. This system demonstrated the incompleteness of any system that can express the relationship between formulas, including the beta and gamma systems. A discussion on whether this result applied to arithmetic systems led to a correspondence between Godel, Carnap

This paper formulates the three balls conjecture in terms of functions $f$ that satisfy certain properties, specifically those related to Clifford analysis. We then demonstrate that these functions, in particular those corresponding to harmonic and monogenic components, can be analyzed within the context of Clifford analysis. Furthermore, we establish relationships between the three balls conjecture and existing theories of harmonic and monogenic function analysis.

The problem of sampling a target set is critical in various applications like data reduction for neural network training, hierarchical clustering, and approximate computational geometric queries. The sequence spatial equidistance sampling problem requires a sequence of samples where the distance between each point and its neighbors remains constant, starting from an initial point without knowledge of the target boundary. This paper introduces a novel approach, the sequential spatial equidistance sampling algorithm, which generates samples in a specific distance pattern. We prove the algorithm's efficiency and show it produces a balanced sample by experimenting with artificial and real-world data, including images. Furthermore, the code for the experiments is available online.

In robotics, adjusting an eye-in-hand camera to capture a specific target is an optimization problem that requires solving various constraints simultaneously. This process can be expensive if done through trial and error, particularly when considering the limitations of the camera's movement. Our approach presents a method for a single camera adjustment policy to be learned from a single target image, using only a small number of possible camera configurations. This is achieved by utilizing a implicit representation of the camera network and adapting the optimization process to work with the inherent ambiguities present in images, using only the intrinsic properties of the camera and target. Our results show that this method can learn a highly efficient and precise policy for adjusting the camera across a wide range of configurations, outperforming a brute force approach, and demonstrating its effectiveness in a real-world application using a UR5 robot.

We tackle an important challenge in mathematical imaging and data analysis, where recovering the original signal is complicated due to limited measurements, noisy data, and unknown measurement processes. A key approach in solving this problem involves the Bayesian framework, which uses stochastic algorithms to estimate the original signal from its observed measurements. The regularization technique is a widely used strategy in signal processing to solve this problem, as it helps strike a balance between fitting the data and reducing the estimated variance. A regularized version of the Conditional Generative Adversarial Network, which incorporates a data-driven regularization, has been recently proposed to solve this problem. Our work builds upon the regularized Conditional GAN by analyzing its connection to Bayesian estimation and suggesting the use of a custom loss function that combines adversarial and Bayesian components. We leverage the advantages of both methods to mitigate the difficulties in simultaneously optimizing the adversarial and Bayesian objectives. Our analysis provides a connection to the Bayesian formulation, especially in its simplified form, and we establish a link between the proposed regularized Conditional GAN and the Bayesian formulation when the measurement process is known. We also explore the benefits of using deep learning architectures, such as the use of over-complete feature maps to regularize the signal, and discuss the challenges faced in obtaining theoretical guarantees of convergence. Our work is motivated by applications in magnetic resonance imaging, specifically in estimating physical properties of biological tissues from MR measurements, such as the water diffusion coefficient and tissue relaxation time.

This article examines the concept of invariant surfaces in fractional dynamical systems, specifically in $n$-dimensional space. It demonstrates that surfaces represented by the equation $f(x_1,...,x_n)=0$ cannot be invariant if the fractional derivative satisfies a certain non-zero condition, even if it is merely defined in terms of the derivative's limit behavior. However, if the surface in question has a specific form, namely $x_1 + |x_2|^{2\alpha} = 0$, then the system can exhibit invariant surfaces in $2$-dimensional space for the frequency $\alpha$ up to $\alpha \leq \frac{1}{2}$.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. However, there are several obstacles to implementing THz communications, mainly the extreme distance that signal waves can travel and the limited capacities of devices to process data. As a result, developing a robust and efficient communication framework that accommodates multiple hops becomes extremely challenging. In this study, we're focusing on optimizing the process of beam training, a critical step in 5G communication where THGMs serve as relay points. We've created a novel approach called Co-OPBT, a cooperative method in which two adjacent THGMs train beams in a coordinated manner. We've also developed a learning algorithm called Q-learning to minimize latency and enhance overall performance. By leveraging simulation data, we've demonstrated that our cooperative approach can result in up to 25 times faster beam training and significantly lower latency compared to existing non-cooperative methods.

The interstellar medium is home to many mysteries, including the properties of the medium in the line of sight to the Earth. Pulsar scintillation observations provide a window into the medium along the line of sight to the pulsar and Earth. By analyzing these observations, we determined the conditions in the line of sight to the Earth-pulsar line of sight for a 11 GHz frequency band. Our analysis used data from the JBO telescope and covered a 1.7 year period, allowing us to detect variations in the medium over time. We discovered that the medium changed in less than 100 days, confirming a previous finding, and found an average timescale for variations of 287 days. We also found an average scale length for variations of 3.5 AU, and found a correlation between the medium and the solar cycle. We did not find a correlation between the position angle and the scintillation pattern, or a variation in the scintillation pattern over a 1.7 year period. Additionally, we estimated the structure function for variations in the medium over a 1.7 year period, and found a value of 0.047.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network is optimized with a quasi-periodic loss function that utilizes a pitch-dependent expanded convolution layer to model periodic signal components. Secondly, a conditional batch normalization layer is integrated with a soft label based on the input pitch, facilitating coordinate information sharing among parallel layers. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the improved pitch control of QPNet in both voice conversion and text-to-speech tasks, showcasing the potential of this model to generate high-quality audio mimicking the spectral and temporal characteristics of target speakers.

This research presents a novel web-based platform called MADARi, which serves as a comprehensive tool for a collaborative task involving the morphological annotation and spelling correction of Modern Standard Arabic. The development process of this platform addressed several challenges associated with the complexities of Arabic script and morphology. To evaluate the effectiveness of MADARi, a pilot study was conducted with a group of undergraduate students who utilized the platform to correct pre-tagged Arabic texts. The results showed that the corrections made by the students using MADARi outperformed those made using a standalone application. Moreover, a further examination was conducted on a larger scale with a diverse set of annotators and obtained statistically significant improvements in accuracy. Furthermore, an experiment was conducted to compare the annotations produced by MADARi with those created through a supervised approach using a rule-based system and Machine Learning techniques.

Planets that orbit close to their stars in temperate zones on planets with conditions similar to those of Earth have a high potential for hosting liquid water and life. However, the presence of a star significantly alters these planets' atmospheric conditions, interacting with photochemical processes that are induced by the star's radiation. This cross-talk between atmospheric components and photochemical reactions affects the composition, temperature, and overall behavior of these extraterrestrial worlds. It also has implications for the absorption and emission spectra of these planets, which can influence the detection and characterization of such worlds using upcoming missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission. Considering various possible photochemical processes and stellar types, our model shows that the composition of these planets can vary based on their size, atmosphere, and relationship to their star. This model also predicts the spectral characteristics of these planets, which can be observed from space using techniques such as spectroscopy. It demonstrates how such observations can be used to determine the presence of photochemical changes, as well as other attributes of these planets, which is essential for understanding their potential for supporting life.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves combining tunneling spectroscopy and study of Ohmic dissipation using resistive electrodes. These studies are particularly relevant for highly-sensitive, low-TFET-voltage techniques that are currently being explored. Ohmic dissipation is a heat generated by tunneling, which can be measured using resistive electrodes in contact with the sample. This measurement allows for distinguishing between a Majorana peak and other peaks based on the ratio of tunneling conductance to generated power. This distinction relies on the difference in tunneling conductance and power generation between a Majorana peak and other peaks, which arises from the non-linear relationship between tunneling conductance and energy when a Majorana peak is present. Additionally, this method can also differentiate between a Majorana peak that is unstable and a stabilization-induced peak by considering the ratio in different tunneling conditions. Furthermore, this method can be combined with phase-sensitive measurements such as tunneling magnetometry to confirm the presence of a Majorana peak.

The development of advanced construction materials and the expansion of road infrastructure to support a growing population of vehicles have increased maintenance costs on roads. Both governments and construction companies are seeking solutions that can automate the road maintenance process, making it more efficient and cost-effective. To address this challenge, we present a groundbreaking technology, called RoadAtlas, an automated system for detecting defects on roads. Based on machine learning principles, RoadAtlas utilizes image data collected from vehicle-mounted cameras to identify flaws in the road, including cracks, potholes, and other issues. This system leverages deep learning algorithms, specifically designed for road defect detection, to analyze images taken at variable speeds and distances. With a robust database of over 5000 training images, RoadAtlas has demonstrated a high level of accuracy in identifying road defects, especially hard-to-detect potholes. Our technology offers a scalable and modular design, enabling easy integration with vehicles equipped with sensors and GPS systems. Furthermore, RoadAtlas includes a user-friendly web interface for managing road data and identifying areas that require maintenance. By automating the road defect detection process, RoadAtlas can help reduce maintenance costs, minimize the risk of accidents caused by poor road conditions, and enable data-driven decisions in road asset management.

The shadow theorem for oriented surfaces has far-reaching implications in many areas of topology and geometry. Despite being a fundamental concept, the shadow theorem lacks a comprehensive proof that accounts for the underlying properties of surfaces. In this paper, we provide a bicategorical interpretation of the shadow theorem that enhances its theoretical significance. Our work builds upon the framework of graded monoidal functors developed by the first author and G.M. Kelly. We establish that the category of surface decorations forms a bicategory when surface edges are categorized as distinct left and right edges. This distinction enables the derivation of the shadow theorem through straightforward categorical proofs. Our findings demonstrate that the shadow theorem is an inherent consequence of surface decoration properties. This approach also facilitates the generalization of the shadow theorem to oriented manifolds with boundary by applying the principles of graded monoidal functors.

Our research seeks to address the challenging task of identifying and erasing misleading image information that influences the accuracy of object detection models. These models are already well-established and widely used for tasks like image classification, but their performance can be severely impacted by noisy annotations and real-world image clutter. Our proposed approach, which we've dubbed "Hard Noise Supervision," is designed to flag and exclude difficult-to-interpret image regions that hinder the training of these models. During training, our method automatically pinpoints uncertain areas that may contain noisy data and adjusts the loss function to ignore these regions. As a result, our model excels in datasets with ambiguous or cluttered images, outperforming the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin on the AICity dataset and surpassing the baseline model on the VOC dataset.

Current graph neural networks operate within non-Euclidean space, powered by the symmetric positive semi-definite matrix embedding that multiple operators can seamlessly compose. Notably, the combination of these embeddings mirrors the cumulative effect of successive Lorentzian transformations along the geometric path connecting two nodes, capturing local patterns inherent in the graph. Nonetheless, existing methods fail to leverage the unique properties of the Lorentzian metric, particularly the metric's asymmetry, congruent transformations, and causal connection, which are vital components of graph inductive representation. Our proposed Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks (LGNNs) framework successfully integrates the Lorentzian metric into the neural network architecture, incorporating the benefits of asymmetry, congruence, and causality into the learning process. Furthermore, our framework is versatile and can be applied to multiple graph classification tasks via the incorporation of a simple global operator, which is itself a geometric descriptor that captures the global structure of the graph. Our experiments demonstrate LGNNs to be an exceptionally effective method for graph classification, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art models on Cora, Citeseer, PubMed, and Bio, with notable improvements made on WebKB and Texas for smaller node counts.

The goal of an inverse problem is to determine a system's properties given its behavior under external influences. Formulating an inverse problem as a optimization problem is a common approach, often requiring the development of a mathematical model that links the system's properties to its observed behavior, and then using optimization algorithms to identify the system's properties. This task becomes even more complicated when the system in question involves an interaction between two different types of phenomena, such as structural and acoustic processes, especially if the underlying mathematical equations are complex and there are limitations on the quality of the available data. This paper presents the difficulties that researchers and engineers encounter when tackling inverse problems in such multi-disciplinary systems, highlighting the challenges posed by the intricate physics involved, limited access to certain system components, and the presence of noise in the data, and it outlines a specific problem related to acoustic structure interaction that any proposed method would need to tackle.

In optomechanical systems, we've observed the transfer of mechanical energy into a laser cavity and its associated electromagnetic field. A key challenge lies in achieving a significant amount of energy being transferred to a narrow-band electromagnetic field, typically requiring a highly tunable filter to align frequencies. This issue becomes even more pronounced when considering the conversion of microwave energy into optical energy. A novel three-part system, consisting of a superconducting circuit, a microwave cavity, and a laser cavity, has shown the ability to efficiently transfer energy to a narrow-band electromagnetic field. This system allows for energy to be transferred over a wide range of frequencies and subsequently compressed into a narrow band, potentially leading to a dramatic increase in the conversion efficiency of optomechanical systems.

We update the basic $\mu$-calculus to accommodate a limited concept of entity quantification, making it possible to express modal logic with transitive closure and entity quantification over finite sets. This updated calculus can also be applied to linear-time logic with finite-set quantification. Additionally, the addition of entity quantification does not increase the complexity of model checking, which remains PSPACE-complete.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating the effects of impulsivity and anxiety, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, while demonstrating that the Tsallis model can be a measure of entropy changes. Furthermore, we provide a mathematical basis for the Tsallis distribution's applicability in the context of delay discounting.

When combining the Hefty gravity theory with gauge invariant operators, specific harmonic gauge choices are made in a way that the Bianchi identities are satisfied. This results in the appearance of a specific gauge field that acts as a bridge between the metric and the gravitational gauge vector. Interestingly, this field has a direct link to the field that appears in the de Rham Bonzom Gleyse Tannar, - gravity model. Furthermore, we show that by making a particular harmonic gauge choice, the Hefty gravity theory reduces to a general covariant theory.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and coloring. By examining the notion of Extended Double Covers, recently proposed by researchers, this work delves deeper into understanding the relationships between planar signed graphs and their connections to the Four-Color Theorem. The authors present a new conjecture, stating that certain graphs which allow homomorphisms to any planar signed graph, will themselves also be able to receive homomorphisms to any planar signed graph, and then prove a related theorem for a certain subclass of graphs without a K_4 minor, and explore near optimal bounds for other subclasses. Additionally, this work introduces the idea of assigning weights to the polarity of edges in a graph, expanding the definition of a signed graph.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representation. Additionally, both the Weyl-Wigner representations and the variable change reveal the classical analogs of key quantum concepts, such as the quantum noise operators and the Fock and coherent states.

I would like to express my appreciation to the organizers for inviting me to give this lecture, which serves as an introduction to the topic of negative absolute temperature. I will begin by defining negative absolute temperature and its distinguishing features, then discuss its conceptual foundations, before moving on to examine its practical applications, including the avoidance of wave function collapse and quantum thermodynamic systems' operation.

Let $k$ be a positive integer, and consider the set of integers modulo $k$. Suppose we have a collection of $n$ subsets of $\mathbb{Z}_k$, denoted as $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$. Define the sum of these subsets as the collection of outcomes after adding the elements together, where the operation used is addition modulo $k$. With this understanding, let's examine the quantity $\sum_{A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n} 1$, where the sum is taken over all possible combinations of $n$ subsets from $\{\mathbb{A}_1,\mathbb{A}_2,\ldots,\mathbb{A}_n\}$, with the constraint that the signed sum of the subsets equals $0$. Our research aims to determine not only the maximum value of $\sum_{A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n} 1$, denoted as $S_k(n)$, but also explore its connection to a well-known problem involving the distribution of integers, specifically the quantity $S_k(n)$ in relation to $k^n/2$.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to determine patient risk and appropriate treatment, but there is a shortage of skilled pathologists to accurately analyze these tissue samples at a high rate. To bridge this gap, we have trained a classification model and a regression model to automate the analysis of these samples based on whole-slide images, using a large dataset of labeled images that we have made publicly available for future researchers to build upon. This dataset, called UniToPatho, contains over 2700 annotations for classifying polyps as normal, hyperplastic, serrated adenoma, or carcinoma, and for grading adenomas based on their severity. We have also published guidelines on how to extend the dataset with more specific classifications of carcinomas and grade levels of serrated adenomas. Our classification model achieved a high accuracy of 94.76% and a low loss age of 5.23% among a test group of 276 samples, while our regression model performed well on benchmark datasets of whole-slide images, reaching a low mean squared error of 0.0467. Notably, our classification model ranked among the top submissions to the 2021 MICCAI Grand Challenge on Adenoma Detection and Classification, and our data suggests that a combination of weakly supervised learning and the extensive UniToPatho dataset could further improve the accuracy of these models.

A novel numerical method has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method, tailored for frequencies much higher than the inhomogeneity wave number, utilizes a time-domain solution strategy, finite elements with a resiliently designed mesh, and a hybrid Fourier-Boundary Element approach to compute the fundamental solution at each frequency. A key aspect of this method is a finite element mesh adaptation that takes advantage of the short-range interaction between the scattered and incident wave components, resulting in a more efficient use of computational resources. To achieve this, the mesh is designed to only capture the wave's local high-frequency behavior near the inhomogeneity, thus allowing for the utilization of finite elements despite the highly oscillatory nature of the solution. Notably, this method can be applied to both source-driven scattering problems and the analysis of incident plane waves, and is suitable for large-scale simulations due to the use of algebraic multigrid methods for solving the linear system.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes, we used thermal metamorphism, annealing, and impact melting to model the water content and isotopic composition. The results indicated that in cases like Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, temperatures likely ranged from 400 to 800$^\circ$C, exceeding average temperatures needed for dehydration in mid-mass radius regions. This implies that accretion of inner solar system planetesimals might have involved low-temperature dust growth processes. We used the water content and isotopic signatures in combination with dust growth models to interpret the results. Our analysis suggested that in cases like Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, the water content and isotopic signatures could be explained by low-temperature dust growth at 1 AU within a few $10^5$ years, with only minimal water incorporation ($\le$0.1 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O).

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ lattices, derived from combining two-chain systems. This results in an affine quantum-group symmetry appearing in the limit of infinite lattice sites. Additionally, explicit formulas are derived for two-particle form factors of single-site operators in the XXZ model, facilitated by an algebraic approach that leverages quantum-group symmetry. This methodology is also adaptable to obtaining super-lattice form factor expressions.

Translation between languages is well represented by supervised machine learning models, yet cross-domain translation (translation into a different modality) remains an unsolved problem in artificial intelligence. Our novel approach presents a method to practice zero-shot translation between languages and speech. We established a single text-to-text translation framework capable of transforming any language to any speech, using a speech dataset that encompasses a wide range of languages. Our data shows that speech translation outperforms previous models and surpasses our baseline speech-to-speech translation model.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime.

This study introduces an expansion of linearized Schur operators in terms of quantum immanents, resulting in double Young-Capelli bitableaux when combined with the elementary symmetric polynomials. These quantum immanents form a basis for the Grothendieck operator, and they align with Kaplansky's noncommutative version of Hilbert's theorem. By applying the classical duality concept, this expansion is shown to be equivalent to shifted Schur symmetric polynomials. A link with the extended Cartan matrix is established through the quantum immanents' own duality property, and a connection with the Rui-Weng graph invariant is revealed via the sum of these quantum immanents over all symmetrization orders.

We've upgraded the scalar sector of the scoto-seesaw model to incorporate two simple, symmetrical groups of Higgs bosons with different electrical charges. This modified model simplifies the neutral component mixing, thereby raising the likelihood of maintaining the Higgs vacuum stable for an appropriate parameter range. Furthermore, we've incorporated a minimal dark matter sector consisting of WIMP particles and analyzed their present-day density, finding that a suitable range exists even without introducing a lepton number transmission. The model exhibits the Higgs vacuum stable for an appropriate parameter range, compatible with the LHC findings, and suitable WIMP dark matter.

We examine the distinction between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals in 3d transition metal oxides and investigate their overlap in higher d-shell transitions. Utilizing the effective crystal field model, we explore how the spin-exchange and correlation terms influence the electron motion in 4d and 5d compounds. A semi-analytical approach allows us to identify the crossover levels at which $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ wave functions significantly mix. The implications of this mixing are analyzed for two instances: (i) strong Hund's mechanism, where the energy levels are lowered due to the mixed character, and (ii) two-dimensional antiferromagnetic arrangements, which can give rise to singlet ground states even without external stress. The study provides a framework for understanding the diverse behaviors observed in 4d and 5d compounds and highlights the necessity for crystal electronic structure and multi-orbital physics in their analysis.

Quantum field theories exhibit non-trivial behavior under transformations that mix physical observables, reflecting underlying symmetries of spacetime. Researchers have identified the underlying principles of this phenomenon, tying it to the concepts of topological charges and geometric symplectic forms. A key aspect is the existence of a relative quantum geometry, which encapsulates the structure of spacetime and is invariant under certain transformations known as wall-crossing. This paper delves into the specifics of how relative quantum geometry behaves under a particular type of transformation called birational transformations. By understanding the intricate relationships between Fock-Goncharov coordinates and the scattering matrix, the paper demonstrates that the relative quantum geometry remains unchanged following such transformations. In essence, this shows that quantum field theories possess an intrinsic symmetry mirrored in the structure of spacetime itself.

A cutting-edge approach to visually enhancing medical images, specifically chest X-rays, is presented in this paper. These enhancements have the potential to create a more convincing and realistic visual theme for data augmentation in machine learning applications. Rather than applying random transformations, the proposed method uses a combination of automatic adjustments and realistic manipulations to augment images. This approach is particularly useful for training models that are sensitive to over-smoothing caused by frequent use of batch normalization. The method is efficient, easy to implement, and produces a diverse range of augmented images. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through improved classification performance compared to random augmentation methods.

ViDaExpert is an advanced tool for multidimensional data visualization and advanced analysis. It's designed to handle vectorial data of any length in multiple dimensions, making it a versatile platform for various data sets, including document and gene expression analyses. The framework is highly customizable, allowing users to easily integrate their own algorithms, methods, and domain-specific knowledge into the tool. A user-friendly web interface, ViDaExpert is an effective solution for high-dimensional data visualization and analysis at large scales, particularly suitable for large-scale document and gene expression analyses.

We have developed an efficient method for computing potentials and forces associated with circular, annular, and combined circular areas in two-dimensional space. By leveraging Green's theorem, we've adapted the fast Fourier transform technique initially proposed in [1] for use with any planar region. This approach enables a rapid evaluation of Newtonian potentials and corresponding forces. The time complexity of this method is O(k log(2n)), where n represents data points, and k corresponds to the number of segments in a given region. To facilitate implementation, our algorithm includes specific directions for constructing Fourier transforms in complex spaces.
